Now I have a good picture. Let me also look at the Sacramento Bee editorial in support and the Mercury News / San Diego Union-Tribune / OC Register editorials against, to weigh the arguments. Also check the League of Women Voters' Easy Voter Guide recommendation.

Also, key considerations:

Arguments FOR Prop 5:
1. The two-question recall allows a replacement to win with a plurality — sometimes a small fraction of votes (2021: leading replacement candidate had ~28% of recall voters; 2003: Schwarzenegger won with 48.6% of the replacement vote, but that was ~31% of all ballots cast). This is undemocratic — the replacement could win with far fewer votes than those cast against the recall. In 2003, more people voted "no recall" (55.4%) than voted for Schwarzenegger (48.6% of replacement vote = ~31% of all ballots). That is a genuine democratic legitimacy problem.
2. Simplifies ballot, reduces cost of printing 100+ candidates.
3. Most other states with recalls use succession/special election, not a same-day replacement.
4. Reduces incentive to use recalls as a "redo" of a prior election — i.e., a partisan weapon.
5. Reduces confusion for voters.
6. Also: Prop 5 removes the Lieutenant Governor's conflict of interest in gubernatorial recalls (SoS now performs recall duties instead of the Lt. Gov, who would directly benefit from the Governor's removal). That's a real good-governance improvement.
7. Endorsed by League of Women Voters of California, California Common Cause, Dan Schnur (former FPPC chair, a Republican/independent). Sacramento Bee endorsed.
8. Passed the Legislature with strong bipartisan-ish margins (Senate 32-8, Assembly 59-17).

Arguments AGAINST Prop 5:
1. Takes away voters' right to choose a replacement directly; transfers power to politicians (the Governor appoints replacements for other statewide offices; the Lt. Governor — same ticket effectively — becomes Governor).
2. A recalled officer could run in the special election to regain the seat — a genuinely bizarre provision that weakens the recall's teeth. Even the author couldn't explain it. SF Chronicle rejected the measure primarily on this basis.
3. The Lt. Governor succeeding a recalled Governor could mean the recall produces no policy change — the person most closely aligned with the recalled governor takes over. Though in California the Lt. Gov is elected separately and could be of a different party.
4. If a Governor is recalled late in the term (after the first two years), the Lt. Governor serves out the remainder of the term with no voter input — potentially up to ~2 years.
5. Creates gaps in representation for legislative seats (months vacant) and could cost millions for separate special elections.
6. Partisan motivation: Democrats advanced it after the 2021 Newsom recall scare; it would have prevented Schwarzenegger (R) from becoming Governor in 2003.
7. It doesn't address the actual root problem (low signature threshold, plurality replacement winner) — a better reform would be a runoff requirement for the replacement or raising signature thresholds.
8. Mercury News, San Diego Union-Tribune, OC Register, SF Chronicle opposed.
9. Polling: 45% yes / 52% no (PPIC October) — trending up but below majority.

Let me think about which side is stronger on the merits.

Core question: Is removing the replacement question a net democratic improvement?

The strongest pro argument is real: In 2003, Gray Davis was recalled with 55.4% voting "yes recall" — but Schwarzenegger got only 48.6% of the replacement vote, which was about 31% of all votes cast. That means ~70% of voters did NOT vote for him. And critically, the recall question and the replacement question were decided by different majorities. A candidate who could never win a normal election can win a recall. Also, in 2021, Larry Elder got 45% of replacement votes, which was ~28% of total recall voters.

But is the current system actually worse than the Prop 5 alternative? Under Prop 5:
- Governor recalled late in term → Lt. Governor serves up to 2 years without any election. The Lt. Governor in California is elected separately, so in principle voters chose them statewide. But they are almost always a co-partisan of the governor, and typically from the same administration's wing. So a successful recall could result in zero change of direction — which arguably defeats the purpose.
- Other statewide officers recalled → Governor appoints replacement. So a partisan ally of the incumbent Governor picks the replacement for a recalled officer. Notably, if the recalled officer is, e.g., the Secretary of State or Attorney General (whom voters may have recalled because of misconduct), the Governor appoints the successor. That's a real democratic deficit. Though this mirrors the existing vacancy process.
- Legislators recalled → special election, but the recalled legislator can run again. This is the biggest flaw. A recall that costs millions and results in the same person potentially returning to office is a seriously weakened accountability tool. And under current law, that's expressly prohibited.

So Prop 5 removes a real flaw (plurality replacement winner) but introduces/retains another real flaw (recalled official can run again; Lt. Gov succession with no voter input late in term).

Now, how often does this matter? Recalls are rare — 11 qualified since 1913, 6 succeeded. So the practical stakes are low. The fiscal impact is negligible (<0.1% of General Fund).

Hmm. Let me think about which is the better vote.

Consider the "worst case" scenarios under each:
- Under current law worst case: An official is recalled by 50%+1 and replaced by someone with 28% of recall voters' support — i.e., someone a supermajority of voters didn't want. This actually happened in spirit in 2003 (Schwarzenegger got 31% of all votes cast). Also produces 135-candidate ballot chaos, ~$200M cost.
- Under Prop 5 worst case: A recalled Governor is replaced by the Lt. Governor (a political ally) for up to 2 years without any election; or a recalled legislator wins the special election right back, nullifying the recall; or a recalled statewide officer is replaced by a gubernatorial appointee with no voter input at all.

Actually the "recalled officer can run again" provision is quite damning — it means the recall becomes an expensive opinion poll rather than an actual removal, in the case of legislators. The author himself admitted "I'm honestly not sure... It wouldn't pain me if it wasn't there." That's a drafting failure at the constitutional level, and constitutional amendments are hard to fix.

Wait — actually let me reconsider. Note the text: "the officer who was the subject of the recall election shall not be appointed to fill the vacancy in that office." So they can't be appointed, but they can run in a special election. For legislators (special elections), that means they can run. For other statewide offices (gubernatorial appointments), they can't be appointed but the Governor could appoint... hmm.

Also — note that in the Governor case, the Lt. Governor becomes Governor for the remainder of the term, with a special election if recalled in the first two years before the close of the nomination period for the next statewide election. Wait, let's re-read: "If the Governor is removed from office by recall before the close of the nomination period for the next statewide election during the first two years of the Governor's term, a special election shall be called to replace the Governor and shall be consolidated with the statewide primary election and, if necessary, the subsequent statewide general election."

So it's a top-two majority-winner special election consolidated with a scheduled statewide primary/general. That's actually a clean, majority-based process. Good.

If recalled in the latter two years, the Lt. Governor serves out the term. Given that the term ends within ~2 years and a regularly scheduled election follows, that's arguably acceptable — comparable to most states.

Hmm. But actually — consider the 2003 case: Gray Davis was recalled in year 1 of his second term (Oct 2003, elected Nov 2002). Under Prop 5, Cruz Bustamante (Dem Lt. Gov) would have become Governor until the March 2004 primary, with a special election. So a Republican wouldn't have won. Democrats see that as restoring majority will; Republicans see it as disenfranchising voters who chose Schwarzenegger.

Let me look at the Sacramento Bee's pro editorial and the Mercury News con editorial to get the strongest versions of each.

Also let me check the League of Women Voters Easy Voter Guide recommendation, and whether there's an IGS/Berkeley poll.

Let me also check: are there other analyses about whether the Lt. Gov could be of a different party? In California, Governor and Lt. Governor are elected on separate ballots. E.g., 1995-1999: Pete Wilson (R) Gov, Gray Davis (D) Lt. Gov. 1983-1995: Deukmejian (R) Gov, Leo McCarthy (D) Lt. Gov. So yes, cross-party is historically possible. That somewhat mitigates the "same team takes over" concern. But recently they've been same-party.

Let me fetch the Sacramento Bee editorial and Mercury News editorial.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: October 20, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 21, 2026 at 11:17 AM PDT

When California Governor Gray Davis was the subject of a recall effort in 2003, he said in a televised speech (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.htmlhttps:/www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.html) at UCLA that he thought the recall would damage “the very fabric of our democracy.”
Elected officials may not like to see accountability arrive earlier than expected, but that doesn’t make Californians’ recall powers a threat to democracy.
While Proposition 5 doesn’t attack the people’s ability to hold a recall election, it does tinker with how a replacement candidate is selected.

Endorsement: Voters should support the Measure M bond to fix Gilroy schools (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-voters-should-support-the-measure-m-bond-to-fix-gilroy-schools/)
We urge voters to reject it.
Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate on the same ballot as a recall. Currently a recall ballot has two questions: 1) Should the elected official be removed, and 2) Choose a candidate to replace that official if the recall is successful.
The measure would remove question 2, eliminating the simultaneous election for a replacement. Instead, if a state official other than a governor was recalled, the office would become vacant and would be filled by special election or appointment, according to existing law. If a governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over and serve until the end of the term or until a special election could be held, depending on timing.
Under current law, a recalled official is barred from running as a replacement candidate in the special election to fill the seat. Proposition 5 changes that as well. In a special election to replace a recalled official, the recalled official could be on the ballot.
These changes turn a process to remove officials from power into a cynical blueprint to keep power in the hands of the same officials. It makes a mockery of the recall, which was designed to empower voters to remove and immediately replace an officeholder for any reason, whether the officeholder thinks the reason is sufficient or not.
Rejecting Proposition 5 is also about preserving the state’s ability to empower unique and independent political voices.
Under current rules, officials who are recalled are succeeded by the candidate seeking that official’s job who gets the most votes at the same time as the recall. This process is why Arnold Schwarzenegger was able to quickly replace the deeply unpopular Davis.
Nearly one million more Californians voted to recall Davis than to retain him, and the Republican Schwarzenegger won a plurality of the replacement vote after running as a pro-business social liberal who wanted the state to lead the global response (https://www.kqed.org/science/1931206/californias-a-team-on-climate-moonbeam-and-the-governator) to climate change.
But if Proposition 5 had been in place, Davis would have been succeeded by Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante. He was an uninspiring but mostly baggage-free politician who would have likely been the favorite in a subsequent regular or special election in California to finish Davis’ term, even against Schwarzenegger.
Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded candidates — while stripping the people of their primary tool of accountability — is a bad idea.
Reject Proposition 5.

Proposition 5 could change California’s recall elections. Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 8:16 AM
Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html) seeks to fundamentally change how California conducts recall elections for members of the Legislature and constitutional officers elected statewide. Such elections have been rare in California.
According to theLegislative Analyst’s Office, (https://lao.ca.gov/) only 11 state recall efforts targeting nine legislators and two governors have qualified for the ballot since 1913. In 2003, Gray Davis (https://www.modbee.com/opinion/opn-columns-blogs/article251385288.html) became the only California governor to be recalled, a fate that also befell five state legislators over the years. The last statewide recall effort to qualify for the ballot was the unsuccessful campaign to oust Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/editorials/article253266413.html)
Under current law, voters are asked two questions in the same election when a recall effort qualifies for the ballot. The first is whether a state officer should be recalled. The second is who should replace that officer from a field of hopefuls seeking consideration if a recall is successful. In 2003, 135 candidates wanted to succeed Davis. In 2021, there were 46 candidates vying for Newsom’s job.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html)
If Prop. 5 is approved by state voters in November, the second question will be eliminated.
In future statewide recalls that gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot, Californians would only vote yes or no on whether an officer should be recalled. If a state recall of a member of the Legislature was successful, that office would remain vacant until a special election was held. If a constitutional officer were recalled, the vacancies would be filled by the governor. Should a future governor be recalled in the first two years of office, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until a special election was held. If a governor were recalled later in the term, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until the next scheduled election.
This would be a longer process, but also one that’s more thoughtful, deliberate and — most importantly — respects the democratic norm of majority rule.
It’s why our combined editorial boards representing The Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee and San Luis Obispo Tribune endorse Prop. 5.
Recall elections in California
Since California voters approved the recall process in 1911, five replacement candidates have been elected after six officials were removed from office with less than 50% of the vote. In California recall elections, the candidate who receives the most votes wins, unlike in a special election, where a candidate must win a majority.
This creates a conundrum of a recalled official garnering more voter support than the replacement candidate who “wins” the recall.
In the 2018 recall of former stateSen. Josh Newman, for instance, (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article145349124.html) his replacement, Republican Ling Ling Chang, came out on top with just under 34% of the vote. Newman points out that he had more votes in his favor; nearly 42% of voters opposed his recall.
“So I got more votes by way of ‘no, don’t kick him out,’ than she got by ‘yes, please put her in,’” Newman said.
Newman won back his Senate seat in the next regular election and then went on to write Prop. 5 (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-voters-prop-5-changes-recall-election-process/73175034).
One of the proposition’s most outspoken opponents is Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a former talk radio host who pushed for Newman’s recall in 2017.
How Prop. 5 opponents feel
DeMaio sees Prop. 5 as an attempt by the ruling party to evade recalls. “What they want to do is create a situation where politicians trying to fend off a recall can say, ‘Don’t vote for the recall or else you won’t be represented for 12 months. You’ll lose your voice,’” he told us.
Actually, Article II, Section 15 of the California Constitution, says a recall election must be held within 60 and 80 days of recall petition signatures being certified. The election may be held within 180 days of certification if it is consolidated with the next regularly scheduled election.
Arguments against Prop. 5 ignore that the current system created instances where replacement candidates got elected with less than 50% of the vote.
They decry the cost of conducting special elections and oppose that Prop. 5 would allow a recalled official to run in a special election to fill the vacancy.
There have been 182 attempts (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present) to recall state officials in California. Eleven of those made the ballot, and only six were successful.
Some view the current recall system as “a weapon for political operators (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5.pdf) to undo election results they don’t like,” to quote the League of Women Voters and others.
Prop. 5 cannot put an end to the political gamesmanship, but it can safeguard the will of the voters by following the principle of majority rule.
McClatchy Media’s California editorial board strongly urges a “yes” vote on Proposition 5.

Proposition 5 could change California’s recall elections. Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 8:16 AM
Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html) seeks to fundamentally change how California conducts recall elections for members of the Legislature and constitutional officers elected statewide. Such elections have been rare in California.
According to theLegislative Analyst’s Office, (https://lao.ca.gov/) only 11 state recall efforts targeting nine legislators and two governors have qualified for the ballot since 1913. In 2003, Gray Davis (https://www.modbee.com/opinion/opn-columns-blogs/article251385288.html) became the only California governor to be recalled, a fate that also befell five state legislators over the years. The last statewide recall effort to qualify for the ballot was the unsuccessful campaign to oust Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/editorials/article253266413.html)
Under current law, voters are asked two questions in the same election when a recall effort qualifies for the ballot. The first is whether a state officer should be recalled. The second is who should replace that officer from a field of hopefuls seeking consideration if a recall is successful. In 2003, 135 candidates wanted to succeed Davis. In 2021, there were 46 candidates vying for Newsom’s job.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html)
If Prop. 5 is approved by state voters in November, the second question will be eliminated.
In future statewide recalls that gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot, Californians would only vote yes or no on whether an officer should be recalled. If a state recall of a member of the Legislature was successful, that office would remain vacant until a special election was held. If a constitutional officer were recalled, the vacancies would be filled by the governor. Should a future governor be recalled in the first two years of office, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until a special election was held. If a governor were recalled later in the term, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until the next scheduled election.
This would be a longer process, but also one that’s more thoughtful, deliberate and — most importantly — respects the democratic norm of majority rule.
It’s why our combined editorial boards representing The Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee and San Luis Obispo Tribune endorse Prop. 5.
Recall elections in California
Since California voters approved the recall process in 1911, five replacement candidates have been elected after six officials were removed from office with less than 50% of the vote. In California recall elections, the candidate who receives the most votes wins, unlike in a special election, where a candidate must win a majority.
This creates a conundrum of a recalled official garnering more voter support than the replacement candidate who “wins” the recall.
In the 2018 recall of former stateSen. Josh Newman, for instance, (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article145349124.html) his replacement, Republican Ling Ling Chang, came out on top with just under 34% of the vote. Newman points out that he had more votes in his favor; nearly 42% of voters opposed his recall.
“So I got more votes by way of ‘no, don’t kick him out,’ than she got by ‘yes, please put her in,’” Newman said.
Newman won back his Senate seat in the next regular election and then went on to write Prop. 5 (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-voters-prop-5-changes-recall-election-process/73175034).
One of the proposition’s most outspoken opponents is Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a former talk radio host who pushed for Newman’s recall in 2017.
How Prop. 5 opponents feel
DeMaio sees Prop. 5 as an attempt by the ruling party to evade recalls. “What they want to do is create a situation where politicians trying to fend off a recall can say, ‘Don’t vote for the recall or else you won’t be represented for 12 months. You’ll lose your voice,’” he told us.
Actually, Article II, Section 15 of the California Constitution, says a recall election must be held within 60 and 80 days of recall petition signatures being certified. The election may be held within 180 days of certification if it is consolidated with the next regularly scheduled election.
Arguments against Prop. 5 ignore that the current system created instances where replacement candidates got elected with less than 50% of the vote.
They decry the cost of conducting special elections and oppose that Prop. 5 would allow a recalled official to run in a special election to fill the vacancy.
There have been 182 attempts (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present) to recall state officials in California. Eleven of those made the ballot, and only six were successful.
Some view the current recall system as “a weapon for political operators (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5.pdf) to undo election results they don’t like,” to quote the League of Women Voters and others.
Prop. 5 cannot put an end to the political gamesmanship, but it can safeguard the will of the voters by following the principle of majority rule.
McClatchy Media’s California editorial board strongly urges a “yes” vote on Proposition 5.

Proposition 5 could change California’s recall elections. Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 8:16 AM
Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html) seeks to fundamentally change how California conducts recall elections for members of the Legislature and constitutional officers elected statewide. Such elections have been rare in California.
According to theLegislative Analyst’s Office, (https://lao.ca.gov/) only 11 state recall efforts targeting nine legislators and two governors have qualified for the ballot since 1913. In 2003, Gray Davis (https://www.modbee.com/opinion/opn-columns-blogs/article251385288.html) became the only California governor to be recalled, a fate that also befell five state legislators over the years. The last statewide recall effort to qualify for the ballot was the unsuccessful campaign to oust Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/editorials/article253266413.html)
Under current law, voters are asked two questions in the same election when a recall effort qualifies for the ballot. The first is whether a state officer should be recalled. The second is who should replace that officer from a field of hopefuls seeking consideration if a recall is successful. In 2003, 135 candidates wanted to succeed Davis. In 2021, there were 46 candidates vying for Newsom’s job.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html)
If Prop. 5 is approved by state voters in November, the second question will be eliminated.
In future statewide recalls that gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot, Californians would only vote yes or no on whether an officer should be recalled. If a state recall of a member of the Legislature was successful, that office would remain vacant until a special election was held. If a constitutional officer were recalled, the vacancies would be filled by the governor. Should a future governor be recalled in the first two years of office, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until a special election was held. If a governor were recalled later in the term, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until the next scheduled election.
This would be a longer process, but also one that’s more thoughtful, deliberate and — most importantly — respects the democratic norm of majority rule.
It’s why our combined editorial boards representing The Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee and San Luis Obispo Tribune endorse Prop. 5.
Recall elections in California
Since California voters approved the recall process in 1911, five replacement candidates have been elected after six officials were removed from office with less than 50% of the vote. In California recall elections, the candidate who receives the most votes wins, unlike in a special election, where a candidate must win a majority.
This creates a conundrum of a recalled official garnering more voter support than the replacement candidate who “wins” the recall.
In the 2018 recall of former stateSen. Josh Newman, for instance, (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article145349124.html) his replacement, Republican Ling Ling Chang, came out on top with just under 34% of the vote. Newman points out that he had more votes in his favor; nearly 42% of voters opposed his recall.
“So I got more votes by way of ‘no, don’t kick him out,’ than she got by ‘yes, please put her in,’” Newman said.
Newman won back his Senate seat in the next regular election and then went on to write Prop. 5 (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-voters-prop-5-changes-recall-election-process/73175034).
One of the proposition’s most outspoken opponents is Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a former talk radio host who pushed for Newman’s recall in 2017.
How Prop. 5 opponents feel
DeMaio sees Prop. 5 as an attempt by the ruling party to evade recalls. “What they want to do is create a situation where politicians trying to fend off a recall can say, ‘Don’t vote for the recall or else you won’t be represented for 12 months. You’ll lose your voice,’” he told us.
Actually, Article II, Section 15 of the California Constitution, says a recall election must be held within 60 and 80 days of recall petition signatures being certified. The election may be held within 180 days of certification if it is consolidated with the next regularly scheduled election.
Arguments against Prop. 5 ignore that the current system created instances where replacement candidates got elected with less than 50% of the vote.
They decry the cost of conducting special elections and oppose that Prop. 5 would allow a recalled official to run in a special election to fill the vacancy.
There have been 182 attempts (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present) to recall state officials in California. Eleven of those made the ballot, and only six were successful.
Some view the current recall system as “a weapon for political operators (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5.pdf) to undo election results they don’t like,” to quote the League of Women Voters and others.
Prop. 5 cannot put an end to the political gamesmanship, but it can safeguard the will of the voters by following the principle of majority rule.
McClatchy Media’s California editorial board strongly urges a “yes” vote on Proposition 5.

Proposition 5 could change California’s recall elections. Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 8:16 AM
Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html) seeks to fundamentally change how California conducts recall elections for members of the Legislature and constitutional officers elected statewide. Such elections have been rare in California.
According to theLegislative Analyst’s Office, (https://lao.ca.gov/) only 11 state recall efforts targeting nine legislators and two governors have qualified for the ballot since 1913. In 2003, Gray Davis (https://www.modbee.com/opinion/opn-columns-blogs/article251385288.html) became the only California governor to be recalled, a fate that also befell five state legislators over the years. The last statewide recall effort to qualify for the ballot was the unsuccessful campaign to oust Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/editorials/article253266413.html)
Under current law, voters are asked two questions in the same election when a recall effort qualifies for the ballot. The first is whether a state officer should be recalled. The second is who should replace that officer from a field of hopefuls seeking consideration if a recall is successful. In 2003, 135 candidates wanted to succeed Davis. In 2021, there were 46 candidates vying for Newsom’s job.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html)
If Prop. 5 is approved by state voters in November, the second question will be eliminated.
In future statewide recalls that gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot, Californians would only vote yes or no on whether an officer should be recalled. If a state recall of a member of the Legislature was successful, that office would remain vacant until a special election was held. If a constitutional officer were recalled, the vacancies would be filled by the governor. Should a future governor be recalled in the first two years of office, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until a special election was held. If a governor were recalled later in the term, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until the next scheduled election.
This would be a longer process, but also one that’s more thoughtful, deliberate and — most importantly — respects the democratic norm of majority rule.
It’s why our combined editorial boards representing The Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee and San Luis Obispo Tribune endorse Prop. 5.
Recall elections in California
Since California voters approved the recall process in 1911, five replacement candidates have been elected after six officials were removed from office with less than 50% of the vote. In California recall elections, the candidate who receives the most votes wins, unlike in a special election, where a candidate must win a majority.
This creates a conundrum of a recalled official garnering more voter support than the replacement candidate who “wins” the recall.
In the 2018 recall of former stateSen. Josh Newman, for instance, (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article145349124.html) his replacement, Republican Ling Ling Chang, came out on top with just under 34% of the vote. Newman points out that he had more votes in his favor; nearly 42% of voters opposed his recall.
“So I got more votes by way of ‘no, don’t kick him out,’ than she got by ‘yes, please put her in,’” Newman said.
Newman won back his Senate seat in the next regular election and then went on to write Prop. 5 (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-voters-prop-5-changes-recall-election-process/73175034).
One of the proposition’s most outspoken opponents is Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a former talk radio host who pushed for Newman’s recall in 2017.
How Prop. 5 opponents feel
DeMaio sees Prop. 5 as an attempt by the ruling party to evade recalls. “What they want to do is create a situation where politicians trying to fend off a recall can say, ‘Don’t vote for the recall or else you won’t be represented for 12 months. You’ll lose your voice,’” he told us.
Actually, Article II, Section 15 of the California Constitution, says a recall election must be held within 60 and 80 days of recall petition signatures being certified. The election may be held within 180 days of certification if it is consolidated with the next regularly scheduled election.
Arguments against Prop. 5 ignore that the current system created instances where replacement candidates got elected with less than 50% of the vote.
They decry the cost of conducting special elections and oppose that Prop. 5 would allow a recalled official to run in a special election to fill the vacancy.
There have been 182 attempts (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present) to recall state officials in California. Eleven of those made the ballot, and only six were successful.
Some view the current recall system as “a weapon for political operators (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5.pdf) to undo election results they don’t like,” to quote the League of Women Voters and others.
Prop. 5 cannot put an end to the political gamesmanship, but it can safeguard the will of the voters by following the principle of majority rule.
McClatchy Media’s California editorial board strongly urges a “yes” vote on Proposition 5.

## The basics
Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time.
Proposition 5 breaks up that process into two parts, prioritizing the voters’ right to oust an official before selecting a replacement.
## The impact
This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to change the current recall system.
Under the proposed changes, voters would first be asked to choose whether or not to oust an official.
Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date.
In the case of a special election, the former officeholder could run again.
The measure also would designate California’s lieutenant governor as the de facto replacement for a recalled governor until the next term.

Actually, I have enough. Let me do one more search to check LWV easy voter guide and any notable split (e.g., whether any Republicans supported, and Dan Schnur's involvement).

Let me also consider the strength of both sides:

Pro-Prop 5 (strong points):
1. Under current law, a replacement can win with a plurality that is smaller than the vote to keep the official. Concrete example: 2018 Newman recall — Chang won with 34%, while 42% voted "no recall." 2003 — Schwarzenegger won with 48.6% of the replacement vote (only ~31% of all ballots cast) while 44.6% voted "no recall." Actually let's be precise: 2003, "no recall" = 55.4%, Schwarzenegger got 48.6% of the replacement votes. So more people voted to keep Davis than voted for Schwarzenegger. That is a genuine democratic legitimacy defect: the person taking office has less support than the person being removed.
2. This is a documented design flaw. Only ~6-7 other states use the two-question format. Most recall states use succession or a separate special election.
3. Reduces the "circus" incentive — 135 candidates in 2003, celebrity candidates, ~$200M cost.
4. Prop 5's gubernatorial special-election mechanism uses top-two with a majority winner — a much more legitimate mandate than a plurality in a 46-candidate field.
5. Prop 5 also fixes a conflict of interest: currently the Lt. Governor performs the Governor's recall duties (setting the election date etc.) even though the Lt. Governor directly benefits from a successful recall. Prop 5 shifts that to the Secretary of State. That's a genuine good-governance improvement that isn't discussed much.
6. Endorsed by League of Women Voters of California, Common Cause California, Dan Schnur (former Republican FPPC chair), Sec. of State Shirley Weber, Lt. Gov. Kounalakis, California Labor Federation, State Building & Construction Trades Council, CA Democratic Party; Sacramento Bee/McClatchy CA editorial boards (5 papers), George Skelton (LA Times columnist) recommends Yes.
7. Passed with broad legislative support: Senate 32-8, Assembly 59-17.

Anti-Prop 5 (strong points):
1. Removes voters' direct say over replacement; gives appointment power to the Governor for other statewide offices (AG, SoS, Treasurer, Controller, Insurance Commissioner, Supt. of Public Instruction, BOE members?, Lt. Gov.). Note: Actually the Superintendent of Public Instruction vacancy — the Governor appoints. Board of Equalization — hmm. Also judicial. So yes, if a voter recalls, e.g., the Attorney General, the Governor picks the replacement. No voter input at all until the next scheduled election.
2. The Lt. Gov succeeds a recalled Governor, and if recalled in the last 2 years, serves the rest of the term with no election. So a recall could produce zero change in direction — arguably defeating the recall's purpose. (Though the Lt. Gov is separately elected and historically has sometimes been of the opposite party.)
3. The recalled official may run in the special election — a real weakening of accountability, and a provision the author himself couldn't justify. SF Chronicle and Mercury News both cited this.
4. Legislative seats sit vacant for months; potentially millions in extra standalone special-election costs.
5. Partisan origin: Democrats advanced it after the 2021 Newsom recall; had it been law in 2003, Schwarzenegger would not have become Governor.
6. It doesn't address the actual root problems — the low signature threshold (12%/20%) that makes recalls easy to trigger, and it could instead just require a runoff for the replacement question, which would be a simpler, less power-shifting fix.
7. Endorsed against by SF Chronicle, Mercury News/East Bay Times, San Diego Union-Tribune, OC Register, CA Republican Party, Reform California (DeMaio), Election Integrity Project CA, Senate Minority Leader Brian Jones, Assemblymember Joe Patterson.
8. Polling: 45% yes / 52% no (PPIC Oct) — likely to fail.

Now, how do I weigh this?

Key judgment: Which system better serves democratic accountability?

The central pro claim — "replacement wins with less support than the votes to keep the incumbent" — is factually true and a genuine defect. But is Prop 5 the right fix? The obvious, minimal fix would be to keep the two-question format but require the replacement to get a majority (runoff), or to raise the signature threshold. Prop 5 instead eliminates voter choice over the successor entirely and hands it to the Lt. Governor / Governor / a later special election where the ousted official can run again.

Notably, the measure's biggest flaw — the recalled official being allowed to run in the special election — directly undercuts the accountability rationale that supporters lead with. If Prop 5's purpose is to restore the recall to "removing corrupt officials," allowing the removed official to immediately run to reclaim the seat (and to do so with the war chest they built during the recall fight, where incumbents can raise unlimited funds) makes the recall nearly pointless for legislative offices. That's not a minor drafting nit; it's the core mechanism for 80 of the 120 state offices affected (all Assembly and Senate seats). And the author's own admission ("I'm honestly not sure... It wouldn't pain me if it wasn't there") shows the amendment is not carefully drafted — and it's a constitutional amendment, which is very hard to fix.

Additionally, the partisan asymmetry: because Democrats hold virtually all statewide constitutional offices and the Governorship, the succession/appointment mechanism means a successful recall of a statewide Democrat would be filled by another Democrat (either the Lt. Gov or a gubernatorial appointee). So Prop 5 functions in practice as an incumbency-protection measure for the majority party. Even if that's not the intent, it's the effect.

Counter-consideration: How likely is this to actually bite? Recalls are rare (11 in 113 years). And the practical impact of a "no" vote is preserving a system with a known democratic defect.

Under current law (NO):
- Defect: replacement can win with a small plurality, potentially fewer votes than "no recall." Documented twice (2003, 2018).
- Benefit: voters directly choose the successor on the same day; the recall is immediate and complete; no gap in representation; the recalled official cannot run; no gubernatorial appointment power; no automatic Lt. Gov succession that preserves the status quo.

Under Prop 5 (YES):
- Fix: the plurality defect is removed; for the Governor recalled early, there's a proper top-two majority special election; Lt. Gov conflict-of-interest removed from administering a gubernatorial recall.
- New defects: recalled official can run again; Lt. Gov auto-succession for late-term recalls (no voter input up to ~2 years); gubernatorial appointments for other statewide offices (no voter input until next scheduled election); vacancy gaps for legislative seats; possible extra election costs; effective incumbency protection for the majority party.

Weighing: The single most important function of a recall is to let voters change who governs. Prop 5 substantially weakens that in three of four scenarios (governor recalled late → Lt. Gov finishes term; other statewide → Governor appoints; legislator → special election where the recalled person can run again). It only genuinely improves on the democratic-legitimacy dimension.

Also, importantly, the LAO notes Prop 5 could raise costs (standalone special elections) — though the fiscal effect is negligible.

I lean toward the view that Prop 5 is a net negative — it addresses a real but narrow defect while introducing broader accountability problems and, in practice, protecting the party in power. And the fact that the author cannot explain the "recalled official may run again" provision is decisive for me: a constitutional amendment shouldn't be approved with an unexplained provision that guts the accountability it claims to protect.

Let me do a couple more checks to make sure I'm not missing something important — e.g., whether there's any argument that the Lt. Governor in California is elected on a separate ticket (which would mitigate), and check the LWV Easy Voter Guide recommendation. Also let me verify the Mercury News's claim about current law barring a recalled official from running in a special election.

Actually the text confirms: current Art. II Sec. 15(c) says "The officer may not be a candidate" — that's struck out by Prop 5. And Prop 5 adds "the officer who was the subject of the recall election shall not be appointed to fill the vacancy in that office." So yes, confirmed: under Prop 5 the recalled officer CAN be a candidate in the special election, but cannot be appointed.

Let me do one final check on LWV easy voter guide and whether any notable independents/cross-party support exists, plus check the Berkeley IGS poll if any.

Actually, let me also double check one thing that could matter a lot: does Prop 5 apply to local recalls? No — it applies to state officers. Good.

Let me do a final search on the League of Women Voters easy voter guide and one more on expert/opinion analyses.

And Prop 5 adds "the officer who was the subject of the recall election shall not be appointed to fill the vacancy in that office." So yes, confirmed: under Prop 5 the recalled officer CAN be a candidate in the special election, but cannot be appointed.

Let me do one final check on LWV easy voter guide and whether any notable independents/cross-party support exists, plus check the Berkeley IGS poll if any.

Actually, let me also double check one thing that could matter a lot: does Prop 5 apply to local recalls? No — it applies to state officers. Good.

Let me do a final search on the League of Women Voters easy voter guide and one more on expert/opinion analyses.

# Your last-minute guide to Proposition 5: Changing how recall elections work
## The basics
Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time.
Proposition 5 breaks up that process into two parts, prioritizing the voters’ right to oust an official before selecting a replacement.
## The impact
This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to change the current recall system.
Under the proposed changes, voters would first be asked to choose whether or not to oust an official.
Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date.
In the case of a special election, the former officeholder could run again.
The measure also would designate California’s lieutenant governor as the de facto replacement for a recalled governor until the next term.

https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform
Support
Proposition 5 is a constitutional amendment born out of a proposal from the secretary of state's office following the unsuccessful recall of Gov.
Gavin Newsom in 2021.
Secretary of State Shirley Weber told lawmakers her office felt a recall election should focus on whether the elected official should be recalled, not whether other potential candidates would be better in the role.
Democrat Josh Newman, who was successfully recalled from his state Senate seat in 2018, authored the measure, saying it would reduce the 'political gamesmanship' that elevates candidates who otherwise wouldn't receive a majority of votes.
Oppose
Opponents including the California Republican Party and Election Integrity Project, which advocates for voter ID requirements and restrictions on mail-in voting, argue that allowing the lieutenant governor to assume the governor's position if the governor were recalled would dissuade people from participating in a recall election.
Almost all legislative Republicans also opposed it, arguing that it would dilute the power of voters while protecting incumbents.
The current recall process is how former Gov.
Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, was elected in 2006.

[{"type":"reasoning.text","text":"Now I have a very thorough picture. Let me also check the League of Women Voters Easy Voter Guide recommendation and any additional key considerations, like whether the Lt. Gov is elected separately (relevant to whether succession means "same team").

Let me also verify one more thing: the San Diego Union-Tribune editorial and any additional analysis about the "recalled official can run again" issue.

Actually, I have enough. Let me do one more search to check LWV easy voter guide and any notable split (e.g., whether any Republicans supported, and Dan Schnur's involvement).

Let me also consider the strength of both sides:

Pro-Prop 5 (strong points):
1. Under current law, a replacement can win with a plurality that is smaller than the vote to keep the official. Concrete example: 2018 Newman recall — Chang won with 34%, while 42% voted "no recall." 2003 — Schwarzenegger won with 48.6% of the replacement vote (only ~31% of all ballots cast) while 44.6% voted "no recall." Actually let's be precise: 2003, "no recall" = 55.4%, Schwarzenegger got 48.6% of the replacement votes. So more people voted to keep Davis than voted for Schwarzenegger. That is a genuine democratic legitimacy defect: the person taking office has less support than the person being removed.
2. This is a documented design flaw. Only ~6-7 other states use the two-question format. Most recall states use succession or a separate special election.
3. Reduces the "circus" incentive — 135 candidates in 2003, celebrity candidates, ~$200M cost.
4. Prop 5's gubernatorial special-election mechanism uses top-two with a majority winner — a much more legitimate mandate than a plurality in a 46-candidate field.
5. Prop 5 also fixes a conflict of interest: currently the Lt. Governor performs the Governor's recall duties (setting the election date etc.) even though the Lt. Governor directly benefits from a successful recall. Prop 5 shifts that to the Secretary of State. That's a genuine good-governance improvement that isn't discussed much.
6. Endorsed by League of Women Voters of California, Common Cause California, Dan Schnur (former Republican FPPC chair), Sec. of State Shirley Weber, Lt. Gov. Kounalakis, California Labor Federation, State Building & Construction Trades Council, CA Democratic Party; Sacramento Bee/McClatchy CA editorial boards (5 papers), George Skelton (LA Times columnist) recommends Yes.
7. Passed with broad legislative support: Senate 32-8, Assembly 59-17.

Anti-Prop 5 (strong points):
1. Removes voters' direct say over replacement; gives appointment power to the Governor for other statewide offices (AG, SoS, Treasurer, Controller, Insurance Commissioner, Supt. of Public Instruction, BOE members?, Lt. Gov.). Note: Actually the Superintendent of Public Instruction vacancy — the Governor appoints. Board of Equalization — hmm. Also judicial. So yes, if a voter recalls, e.g., the Attorney General, the Governor picks the replacement. No voter input at all until the next scheduled election.
2. The Lt. Gov succeeds a recalled Governor, and if recalled in the last 2 years, serves the rest of the term with no election. So a recall could produce zero change in direction — arguably defeating the recall's purpose. (Though the Lt. Gov is separately elected and historically has sometimes been of the opposite party.)
3. The recalled official may run in the special election — a real weakening of accountability, and a provision the author himself couldn't justify. SF Chronicle and Mercury News both cited this.
4. Legislative seats sit vacant for months; potentially millions in extra standalone special-election costs.
5. Partisan origin: Democrats advanced it after the 2021 Newsom recall; had it been law in 2003, Schwarzenegger would not have become Governor.
6. It doesn't address the actual root problems — the low signature threshold (12%/20%) that makes recalls easy to trigger, and it could instead just require a runoff for the replacement question, which would be a simpler, less power-shifting fix.
7. Endorsed against by SF Chronicle, Mercury News/East Bay Times, San Diego Union-Tribune, OC Register, CA Republican Party, Reform California (DeMaio), Election Integrity Project CA, Senate Minority Leader Brian Jones, Assemblymember Joe Patterson.
8. Polling: 45% yes / 52% no (PPIC Oct) — likely to fail.

Now, how do I weigh this?

Key judgment: Which system better serves democratic accountability?

The central pro claim — "replacement wins with less support than the votes to keep the incumbent" — is factually true and a genuine defect. But is Prop 5 the right fix? The obvious, minimal fix would be to keep the two-question format but require the replacement to get a majority (runoff), or to raise the signature threshold. Prop 5 instead eliminates voter choice over the successor entirely and hands it to the Lt. Governor / Governor / a later special election where the ousted official can run again.

Notably, the measure's biggest flaw — the recalled official being allowed to run in the special election — directly undercuts the accountability rationale that supporters lead with. If Prop 5's purpose is to restore the recall to "removing corrupt officials," allowing the removed official to immediately run to reclaim the seat (and to do so with the war chest they built during the recall fight, where incumbents can raise unlimited funds) makes the recall nearly pointless for legislative offices. That's not a minor drafting nit; it's the core mechanism for 80 of the 120 state offices affected (all Assembly and Senate seats). And the author's own admission ("I'm honestly not sure... It wouldn't pain me if it wasn't there") shows the amendment is not carefully drafted — and it's a constitutional amendment, which is very hard to fix.

Additionally, the partisan asymmetry: because Democrats hold virtually all statewide constitutional offices and the Governorship, the succession/appointment mechanism means a successful recall of a statewide Democrat would be filled by another Democrat (either the Lt. Gov or a gubernatorial appointee). So Prop 5 functions in practice as an incumbency-protection measure for the majority party. Even if that's not the intent, it's the effect.

Counter-consideration: How likely is this to actually bite? Recalls are rare (11 in 113 years). And the practical impact of a "no" vote is preserving a system with a known democratic defect.

Hmm, this is genuinely close. Let me think about which is the better decision.

Let me think about what the "best outcome" is. Neither option is ideal. The question is which is worse.

Under current law (NO):
- Defect: replacement can win with a small plurality, potentially fewer votes than "no recall." Documented twice (2003, 2018).
- Benefit: voters directly choose the successor on the same day; the recall is immediate and complete; no gap in representation; the recalled official cannot run; no gubernatorial appointment power; no automatic Lt. Gov succession that preserves the status quo.

Under Prop 5 (YES):
- Fix: the plurality defect is removed; for the Governor recalled early, there's a proper top-two majority special election; Lt. Gov conflict-of-interest removed from administering a gubernatorial recall.
- New defects: recalled official can run again; Lt. Gov auto-succession for late-term recalls (no voter input up to ~2 years); gubernatorial appointments for other statewide offices (no voter input until next scheduled election); vacancy gaps for legislative seats; possible extra election costs; effective incumbency protection for the majority party.

Weighing: The single most important function of a recall is to let voters change who governs. Prop 5 substantially weakens that in three of four scenarios (governor recalled late → Lt. Gov finishes term; other statewide → Governor appoints; legislator → special election where the recalled person can run again). It only genuinely improves on the democratic-legitimacy dimension.

Also, importantly, the LAO notes Prop 5 could raise costs (standalone special elections) — though the fiscal effect is negligible.

I lean toward the view that Prop 5 is a net negative — it addresses a real but narrow defect while introducing broader accountability problems and, in practice, protecting the party in power. And the fact that the author cannot explain the "recalled official may run again" provision is decisive for me: a constitutional amendment shouldn't be approved with an unexplained provision that guts the accountability it claims to protect.

Let me do a couple more checks to make sure I'm not missing something important — e.g., whether there's any argument that the Lt. Governor in California is elected on a separate ticket (which would mitigate), and check the LWV Easy Voter Guide recommendation. Also let me verify the Mercury News's claim about current law barring a recalled official from running in a special election.

Actually the text confirms: current Art. II Sec. 15(c) says "The officer may not be a candidate" — that's struck out by Prop 5. And Prop 5 adds "the officer who was the subject of the recall election shall not be appointed to fill the vacancy in that office." So yes, confirmed: under Prop 5 the recalled officer CAN be a candidate in the special election, but cannot be appointed.

Let me do one final check on LWV easy voter guide and whether any notable independents/cross-party support exists, plus check the Berkeley IGS poll if any.

Actually, let me also double check one thing that could matter a lot: does Prop 5 apply to local recalls? No — it applies to state officers. Good.

Let me do a final search on the League of Women Voters easy voter guide and one more on expert/opinion analyses.

PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 4:33 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:07 PM PST
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem does Prop. 5 solve?
In its current form, a state-level recall ballot asks two questions in sequence: first, whether to remove an elected official, and second, who should immediately replace them. Although removal requires a majority vote, replacement doesn’t; whoever gets the most votes takes office, even if it’s by a small plurality in a crowded field. That mismatch can mean that an officeholder ousted by majority vote can be replaced by someone with far less support, and it gives well-organized interest groups a powerful incentive to instigate a recall in order to install a preferred candidate who wouldn’t have majority support under normal conditions. Prop. 5 fixes that mismatch by removing the replacement question and filling a vacancy under existing succession law instead.

Why is this the best solution?
Prop. 5 is the best solution because it fixes the specific, politically exploitable flaw — the plurality replacement provision — while still maintaining the recall as a powerful tool of direct democracy. Under its provisions, if a governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor, already duly elected by a majority of Californians statewide, steps in. If a recall takes place in the first two years of the term and before the filing deadline for the next statewide election, voters would still get a special election for a permanent successor, with a runoff if needed to achieve a majority. If the recall takes place later in the term, the lieutenant governor would serve out the remainder of an ousted governor’s term, the same as if they were to leave office for some other reason. In the event of a recall of other state-level officers, those offices would be filled under existing vacancy replacement provisions.
Why would Californians want to remove someone from office but forfeit to the governor their current right to immediately choose a successor?
Two corrections worth making: In the event of a gubernatorial recall, it wouldn’t be the governor who gains power but the lieutenant governor, a separately elected constitutional officer who is, by virtue of California’s Constitution, explicitly and deliberately next in the line of succession. Intrinsic to any lieutenant governor’s campaign is the assertion that he or she is most qualified to step in if events so demand. Second, voters aren’t forfeiting a choice: If a governor is recalled early in their term, Californians would still elect a permanent successor by majority through a special election. This is a sensible change from the current format, where, in the event of a gubernatorial recall, a replacement candidate can become governor of the largest and most important state in the country with only a small plurality, in a special election decided by a reduced electorate in a low-information and highly politicized environment.
Explain how this empowers majority rule and why that matters.
As it currently stands, while recalling a state-level elected official requires majority support, replacing them doesn’t. Only a plurality is required, which could be as low as 20% in a crowded replacement field. Prop. 5 closes that gap. When a successor election is held, if no one wins a majority outright, it would go to a runoff. So, whoever ultimately holds the office would have secured the support of more than half the voters, not just the largest slice of a fractured field. This is the standard California already applies to nearly every other office and election scenario. A recall shouldn’t be the one process where a candidate can take power without the validation of majority voter support.
How does this measure stop political groups from abusing the recall process?
It removes the existing incentive for political gamesmanship at the expense of electoral integrity. As it stands, a well-funded, motivated minority can force a recall and realistically expect its preferred candidate to win the replacement seat with a small plurality, sometimes far fewer votes than the officeholder who was removed. That’s a low bar for a high-value prize, and it’s why some recalls have been criticized as backdoor attempts to grab a seat that couldn’t be won in a regular election. Prop. 5 raises the bar and removes that incentive: Voters will still be able to remove a corrupt or malfeasant official, but it removes the strategic upside of gaming a plurality-only replacement. Instead, a replacement would be made in the normal order, and in the next election, the winner would ultimately secure a majority, with a runoff if needed.
How would this save taxpayers money?
First and foremost, by changing the incentive structure by eliminating the second question, Prop. 5 would save taxpayers money by reducing the likelihood of hyperpartisan recalls like the one which targeted Gov. Newson in 2021, which cost California taxpayers more than $200 million dollars in the midst of an unprecedented public health emergency where those funds were desperately needed for other purposes. Measure to reform the California recall process (YES ON PROP 5) (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2026/10/21/measure-to-reform-the-california-recall-process-yes-on-5/)
Posted on 21/10/2026 (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2026/10/21/measure-to-reform-the-california-recall-process-yes-on-5/) by msshugart (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/author/msshugart/)
In this November’s election, Californians are presented with a proposed state constitutional amendment to reform the process of recalling and replacing elected officeholders. It was placed on the ballot by the state legislature as Proposition 5. I am in favor, and I urge California voters to support it. Below are some excerpts from the voter guide (you can access the whole thing via a click here (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/)).
The main defect in the current process that Prop. 5 would fix is the situation whereby a replacement candidate can be elected with less than a majority, and potentially fewer votes than the NO (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2021/08/15/californias-recall-replacement-rules-are-terrible-but-are-they-unconstitutional/) on the recall (i.e., preferring the incumbent remain in office). The state constitution mandates that offices be filled by majority vote, but makes an exception for the replacement for a recalled officer, who must win only a plurality of votes (contingent on YES having a majority for recall). In an earlier post (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2021/09/15/reforming-the-california-recall-replacement-process/) on this problem, I quoted the specific constitutional provisions. A YES on 5 would directly correct this defect.
Under the proposal in Prop. 5, the office becomes vacant and is filled the same way it would be under current provisions if the officer left the post for any other reason (resigning to take another office, death, etc.): special election or appointment, depending on the office. The exception to this generalization of the impact of Prop. 5 is in the right column of the above table: the case of a Governor being recalled. We have a (separately elected) Lieutenant Governor and that officeholder would replace a recalled Governor. However, if the recall takes place in a period leading up to what would be the midterm election of the incumbent’s term (provided it is before candidate-filing deadline), there would be a special election to fill the remainder of the term. This is a sensible provision.
This measure is not perfect, but it is an improvement over the status quo. No longer would a replacement potentially be elected by a plurality instead of a majority. The biggest flaw I see is that in the case of some offices, such as state legislative seats, 1 it would extend the period of vacancy following a recall, and it would necessitate up to two additional elections to fill the seat. 2
There are other ways that the recall–replacement process could be changed to resolve the current problem that this proposition would correct, without creating the new problem I identified of longer vacancies and additional special elections. I went over several of these in the earlier post on reforming the California recall–replacement process (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2021/09/15/reforming-the-california-recall-replacement-process/). (That post was mainly focused on gubernatorial recalls, and I am happy with the Prop. 5 solution on these; the points I made on suggested reforms are generalizable to other contests as well.)
My main suggestion would be to abolish the separate recall election and simply call a special election when the recall petition has been qualified. If the incumbent were to run to defend his or her seat, the incumbent survives in office simply by winning a plurality of the vote. I call this a “constructive recall.” 3 This encourages the opponents to coordinate before the election, and if they fail, their recall bid fails. If a potential replacement candidate wins a majority, he or she is elected and sworn in immediately. If a potential replacement candidate wins only a plurality, then there is a runoff between the candidates with the two highest vote totals. (At least that is how I would do it as long as we use the “top two (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/category/california/top-two-system-not-a-primary/)” system for regular elections. As I have said many times, I dislike that, but that is a separate discussion and one I have addressed in detail (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2024/08/16/unified-primaries-and-rcv-as-steps-towards-us-house-pr-and-what-about-resistance-to-list-pr/#f5219553-9421-4847-ab31-4699862375a9-link) previously.) No proposed process would be without flaws, 4 but I think something like what I propose here would be better. 5 Nonetheless, what is actually before the voters as Proposition 5 in this election is an improvement on the status quo. So I hope YES on PROP 5 wins.
While we are on the topic of measures concerning election rules on this ballot, I also advocate NO on 43 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) , which if passed would raise to two thirds the vote percentage required for a municipal initiative that would propose or increase taxes for a specific purpose. I am against increasing minority-veto provisions such as this.
________
Other resources on Prop. 5: The yes campaign (https://fixtherecall.com/#press) website, LA Time (https://www.latimes.com/politics/newsletter/2026-09-09/california-recall-election-reform-proposition-5)s op-ed, SacBee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316600442.html) op-ed.
________
The ballot title for the proposition says that it “Changes the recall election process for statewide officers.” However, the text does not seem to leave state legislative seats outside its purview, and the cited section of the constitution clearly deals with state legislators as well as statewide offices. Importantly, the Voter Information Guide (in the screenshot) mentions Assembly and (state) Senate. Even were it to apply only to statewide (and thus executive) posts, everything else I write in this post still would be valid, albeit for a narrower range of cases. ↩︎
A special election in California to fill an interim vacancy (other than in the case of recall) mandates that if one candidate wins a majority of votes, that candidate is elected; otherwise the contest goes to a top-two runoff. ↩︎
Obviously playing off the concept of a constructive vote of no confidence (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/tag/constructive-vote-of-no-confidence/) in some parliamentary democracies, whereby merely losing a vote moved by the opposition is not sufficient to oust an incumbent government. Instead, the parliamentary majority must elect a specific new government. ↩︎
The biggest flaw that comes to mind when thinking of my own proposal here is that it complicates matters for the party of the officer being recalled. That party has to put up a challenger directly against the incumbent, and the split might make the incumbent more likely to survive in office than under the current procedure. However, I do not think that is a great flaw. I am in favor of making it harder to recall, not easier, and in any case, even with separate recall and replacement votes on the same ballot (as is now the case), the incumbent’s party already faces an acute version of this difficulty. Successful recalls are highly likely to change the party holding the office, and that is probably on balance not a bad feature of the process. My proposed procedure has some advantage in encouraging the party of the officeholder to coordinate (whether on the incumbent or a same-party replacement) in addition to encouraging coordination by the opposing forces (as noted above). ↩︎
I would also be on board with a proposal that calls a special election as I describe here but without my “constructive” provision. That is, simply call a special election, under the current procedures used for such election (see footnote 2), without a separate yes/no recall question. ↩︎

California Governor 2026 (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2026/06/02/california-governor-2026/)
Posted on 02/06/2026 (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2026/06/02/california-governor-2026/) by msshugart (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/author/msshugart/)
Election day is finally here. I will not lament the (temporary) end to mailers and TV ads. The governor’s contest in California this year offers a choice of 61 candidates. And yet it somehow does not seem like much of a choice. We have a STUPID (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2022/06/08/californias-stupid-electoral-system-2022-first-round-edition/) electoral system. This is called a primary but is not. It is simple top two, qualifying the two with the highest vote shares regardless of party. By common understanding, a primary election is a party nominating contest, so it should qualify one from each party (and thus more than two). Terminology aside, the strategic incentives (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2024/03/03/california-2024-first-round-and-adam-schiff-for-senate/) and risk of coordination failure (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2024/08/18/a-coordination-failure-followed-by-a-party-switch-cal-sen-4/)are problematic.
Over the course of the campaign there has been a great deal of consternation in Democratic Party circles about the risk that the many candidates on their side could split the vote and allow two Republicans to make it to the runoff. This never seemed remotely plausible to me, even though the rules certainly make it possible. I expected all along that the higher probability was that, despite the fragmentation on their side, it was likelier that two Democrats would make it.
Given that Republicans struggle to get to even 45% of the vote in statewide contests here (and often do much worse), the two Republicans would have to almost perfectly divide their votes, while no Democrat obtained even half the total Republican share. Even with several arguably “serious” candidates, the possibility that none of them would get more than around 22% of the vote seemed unlikely.
And now as we prepare to start seeing actual results, the polling (https://www.270towin.com/2026-governor-polls/california) has come to suggest (https://calmatters.org/newsletter/governor-race-poll-whos-ahead/) that there is the possibly of a close race for second between Democrat Tom Steyer and Republican Steve Hilton. Xavier Becerra, a Democrat, appears to be leading, although some polls have Hilton in first place. Of course, it is that second slot that matters more than who is first. So unless there is a surprise, it probably will come down to a conventional R vs. D runoff (Becerra and Hilton) or two Democrats (Becerra and Steyer).
In the final stages of the campaign, Steyer started unleashing some quite sharp negative attacks on Becerra. It might have made more sense for him to use his ample fortune to attack Hilton, given this is not a purely intraparty contest and he is probably competing realistically for second place.
By the way, I am very open to having comments on this thread on elections happening in other states today, or other California contests aside from the governor race.

Posted on 04/01/2026 (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2026/01/04/ranked-choice-voting-at-the-county-level-in-california-santa-claras-unique-circumstances/) by msshugart (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/author/msshugart/)
This post is a follow-on to the previous one about a low-turnout runoff in Santa Clara County (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2026/01/02/a-very-low-turnout-runoff-santa-clara-county-assessor-2025/), California. Could the county change the election of its officers to ranked-choice voting (via the alternative vote a.k.a. instant runoff)? Yes, it could. However, it is the only county that currently has this authority. Further, it appears it could switch to STV for its Board of Supervisors.
AB 1227 (https://www.leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240AB1227) of 2023 was passed by the state legislature and signed by the governor and explicitly grants to Santa Clara County the option to adopt ranked-choice voting (RCV) for any or all elected county officers. It allows that either the county’s Board of Supervisors or a county initiative may enact RCV.
The legislation further says, “The ordinance [to adopt RCV] shall specify which county officers shall be elected by this method and whether they shall be elected at large or by or from district, as applicable.” The reference to “at large” surely enables the country to elect the Board or other multi-person bodies in the county by single transferable vote (STV), sometimes called (in the US) proportional ranked-choice voting (PRCV). The first section of the enacted state law–the “findings” section–references cities in California that have adopted STV, such as Albany (https://www.albanyca.gov/Departments/City-Clerk/Ranked-Choice-Voting) and Palm Desert (https://www.palmdesert.gov/our-city/election-information), although it simply refers to their systems as “RCV” without the important detail. (Palm Desert now has two districts, one of which is a single seat using RCV/alternative vote, and the other of which elects four by STV/PRCV.)
Interestingly, the law applies only to Santa Clara County. Moreover, its third of three sections reads, in full: “The Legislature finds and declares that a special statute is necessary and that a general statute cannot be made applicable within the meaning of Section 16 of Article IV of the California Constitution because of the unique circumstances relating to the County of Santa Clara’s interest in having the option to use ranked choice voting in its elections.” (The cited section (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2016.&article=IV) states, “A local or special statute is invalid in any case if a general statute can be made applicable.”)
Therefore, we might say that we have here a case “electoral system pork barrel”! Okay it is not a project, which is what “pork barrel” implies, but a measure regarding electoral systems that provides a benefit only to the geographical region represented by its sponsors. The originally introduced bill did not have that third section, although it did already state its applicability was only to the one county. The introducing member was Assembly Member Evan Low, who at the time represented Assembly District 26, encompassing parts of the Silicon Valley, which is to say a large portion of Santa Clara County. Assembly Member Alex Lee later joined as a co-author; his district encompasses other parts of the county, including part of the city of San Jose.

The initial version did not specify the timing of a potential RCV election in the county. A further round of amendments in the Senate saw two members of that chamber join as further coauthors, Josh Becker and David Cortese, both of whom represent–you guessed it–parts of Santa Clara County. However, before its final passage the language to require that any such RCV election in the county be held at the “primary” was included.
