Measure to reform the California recall process (YES ON PROP 5) (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2026/10/21/measure-to-reform-the-california-recall-process-yes-on-5/)
Posted on 21/10/2026 (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2026/10/21/measure-to-reform-the-california-recall-process-yes-on-5/) by msshugart (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/author/msshugart/)
In this November’s election, Californians are presented with a proposed state constitutional amendment to reform the process of recalling and replacing elected officeholders. It was placed on the ballot by the state legislature as Proposition 5. I am in favor, and I urge California voters to support it. Below are some excerpts from the voter guide (you can access the whole thing via a click here (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/)).
The main defect in the current process that Prop. 5 would fix is the situation whereby a replacement candidate can be elected with less than a majority, and potentially fewer votes than the NO (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2021/08/15/californias-recall-replacement-rules-are-terrible-but-are-they-unconstitutional/) on the recall (i.e., preferring the incumbent remain in office). The state constitution mandates that offices be filled by majority vote, but makes an exception for the replacement for a recalled officer, who must win only a plurality of votes (contingent on YES having a majority for recall). In an earlier post (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2021/09/15/reforming-the-california-recall-replacement-process/) on this problem, I quoted the specific constitutional provisions. A YES on 5 would directly correct this defect.
Under the proposal in Prop. 5, the office becomes vacant and is filled the same way it would be under current provisions if the officer left the post for any other reason (resigning to take another office, death, etc.): special election or appointment, depending on the office. The exception to this generalization of the impact of Prop. 5 is in the right column of the above table: the case of a Governor being recalled. We have a (separately elected) Lieutenant Governor and that officeholder would replace a recalled Governor. However, if the recall takes place in a period leading up to what would be the midterm election of the incumbent’s term (provided it is before candidate-filing deadline), there would be a special election to fill the remainder of the term. This is a sensible provision.
This measure is not perfect, but it is an improvement over the status quo. No longer would a replacement potentially be elected by a plurality instead of a majority. The biggest flaw I see is that in the case of some offices, such as state legislative seats, 1 it would extend the period of vacancy following a recall, and it would necessitate up to two additional elections to fill the seat. 2
There are other ways that the recall–replacement process could be changed to resolve the current problem that this proposition would correct, without creating the new problem I identified of longer vacancies and additional special elections. I went over several of these in the earlier post on reforming the California recall–replacement process (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2021/09/15/reforming-the-california-recall-replacement-process/). (That post was mainly focused on gubernatorial recalls, and I am happy with the Prop. 5 solution on these; the points I made on suggested reforms are generalizable to other contests as well.)
My main suggestion would be to abolish the separate recall election and simply call a special election when the recall petition has been qualified. If the incumbent were to run to defend his or her seat, the incumbent survives in office simply by winning a plurality of the vote. I call this a “constructive recall.” 3 This encourages the opponents to coordinate before the election, and if they fail, their recall bid fails. If a potential replacement candidate wins a majority, he or she is elected and sworn in immediately. If a potential replacement candidate wins only a plurality, then there is a runoff between the candidates with the two highest vote totals. (At least that is how I would do it as long as we use the “top two (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/category/california/top-two-system-not-a-primary/)” system for regular elections. As I have said many times, I dislike that, but that is a separate discussion and one I have addressed in detail (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2024/08/16/unified-primaries-and-rcv-as-steps-towards-us-house-pr-and-what-about-resistance-to-list-pr/#f5219553-9421-4847-ab31-4699862375a9-link) previously.) No proposed process would be without flaws, 4 but I think something like what I propose here would be better. 5 Nonetheless, what is actually before the voters as Proposition 5 in this election is an improvement on the status quo. So I hope YES on PROP 5 wins.
While we are on the topic of measures concerning election rules on this ballot, I also advocate NO on 43 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) , which if passed would raise to two thirds the vote percentage required for a municipal initiative that would propose or increase taxes for a specific purpose. I am against increasing minority-veto provisions such as this.
________
Other resources on Prop. 5: The yes campaign (https://fixtherecall.com/#press) website, LA Time (https://www.latimes.com/politics/newsletter/2026-09-09/california-recall-election-reform-proposition-5)s op-ed, SacBee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316600442.html) op-ed.
________
The ballot title for the proposition says that it “Changes the recall election process for statewide officers.” However, the text does not seem to leave state legislative seats outside its purview, and the cited section of the constitution clearly deals with state legislators as well as statewide offices. Importantly, the Voter Information Guide (in the screenshot) mentions Assembly and (state) Senate. Even were it to apply only to statewide (and thus executive) posts, everything else I write in this post still would be valid, albeit for a narrower range of cases. ↩︎
A special election in California to fill an interim vacancy (other than in the case of recall) mandates that if one candidate wins a majority of votes, that candidate is elected; otherwise the contest goes to a top-two runoff. ↩︎
Obviously playing off the concept of a constructive vote of no confidence (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/tag/constructive-vote-of-no-confidence/) in some parliamentary democracies, whereby merely losing a vote moved by the opposition is not sufficient to oust an incumbent government. Instead, the parliamentary majority must elect a specific new government. ↩︎
The biggest flaw that comes to mind when thinking of my own proposal here is that it complicates matters for the party of the officer being recalled. That party has to put up a challenger directly against the incumbent, and the split might make the incumbent more likely to survive in office than under the current procedure. However, I do not think that is a great flaw. I am in favor of making it harder to recall, not easier, and in any case, even with separate recall and replacement votes on the same ballot (as is now the case), the incumbent’s party already faces an acute version of this difficulty. Successful recalls are highly likely to change the party holding the office, and that is probably on balance not a bad feature of the process. My proposed procedure has some advantage in encouraging the party of the officeholder to coordinate (whether on the incumbent or a same-party replacement) in addition to encouraging coordination by the opposing forces (as noted above). ↩︎
I would also be on board with a proposal that calls a special election as I describe here but without my “constructive” provision. That is, simply call a special election, under the current procedures used for such election (see footnote 2), without a separate yes/no recall question. ↩︎

In this November’s election, Californians are presented with a proposed state constitutional amendment to reform the process of recalling and replacing elected officeholders. It was placed on the ballot by the state legislature as Proposition 5. I am in favor, and I urge California voters to support it. Below are some excerpts from the voter guide (you can access the whole thing via a click here (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/)).
The main defect in the current process that Prop. 5 would fix is the situation whereby a replacement candidate can be elected with less than a majority, and potentially fewer votes than the NO (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2021/08/15/californias-recall-replacement-rules-are-terrible-but-are-they-unconstitutional/) on the recall (i.e., preferring the incumbent remain in office). The state constitution mandates that offices be filled by majority vote, but makes an exception for the replacement for a recalled officer, who must win only a plurality of votes (contingent on YES having a majority for recall). In an earlier post (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2021/09/15/reforming-the-california-recall-replacement-process/) on this problem, I quoted the specific constitutional provisions. A YES on 5 would directly correct this defect.
Under the proposal in Prop. 5, the office becomes vacant and is filled the same way it would be under current provisions if the officer left the post for any other reason (resigning to take another office, death, etc.): special election or appointment, depending on the office. The exception to this generalization of the impact of Prop. 5 is in the right column of the above table: the case of a Governor being recalled. We have a (separately elected) Lieutenant Governor and that officeholder would replace a recalled Governor. However, if the recall takes place in a period leading up to what would be the midterm election of the incumbent’s term (provided it is before candidate-filing deadline), there would be a special election to fill the remainder of the term. This is a sensible provision.
This measure is not perfect, but it is an improvement over the status quo. No longer would a replacement potentially be elected by a plurality instead of a majority. The biggest flaw I see is that in the case of some offices, such as state legislative seats, 1 it would extend the period of vacancy following a recall, and it would necessitate up to two additional elections to fill the seat. 2
There are other ways that the recall–replacement process could be changed to resolve the current problem that this proposition would correct, without creating the new problem I identified of longer vacancies and additional special elections. I went over several of these in the earlier post on reforming the California recall–replacement process (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2021/09/15/reforming-the-california-recall-replacement-process/). (That post was mainly focused on gubernatorial recalls, and I am happy with the Prop. 5 solution on these; the points I made on suggested reforms are generalizable to other contests as well.)
My main suggestion would be to abolish the separate recall election and simply call a special election when the recall petition has been qualified. If the incumbent were to run to defend his or her seat, the incumbent survives in office simply by winning a plurality of the vote. I call this a “constructive recall.” 3 This encourages the opponents to coordinate before the election, and if they fail, their recall bid fails. If a potential replacement candidate wins a majority, he or she is elected and sworn in immediately. If a potential replacement candidate wins only a plurality, then there is a runoff between the candidates with the two highest vote totals. (At least that is how I would do it as long as we use the “top two (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/category/california/top-two-system-not-a-primary/)” system for regular elections. As I have said many times, I dislike that, but that is a separate discussion and one I have addressed in detail (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2024/08/16/unified-primaries-and-rcv-as-steps-towards-us-house-pr-and-what-about-resistance-to-list-pr/#f5219553-9421-4847-ab31-4699862375a9-link) previously.) No proposed process would be without flaws, 4 but I think something like what I propose here would be better. 5 Nonetheless, what is actually before the voters as Proposition 5 in this election is an improvement on the status quo. So I hope YES on PROP 5 wins.
While we are on the topic of measures concerning election rules on this ballot, I also advocate NO on 43 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) , which if passed would raise to two thirds the vote percentage required for a municipal initiative that would propose or increase taxes for a specific purpose. I am against increasing minority-veto provisions such as this.
________
Other resources on Prop. 5: The yes campaign (https://fixtherecall.com/#press) website, LA Time (https://www.latimes.com/politics/newsletter/2026-09-09/california-recall-election-reform-proposition-5)s op-ed, SacBee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316600442.html) op-ed.
________
The ballot title for the proposition says that it “Changes the recall election process for statewide officers.” However, the text does not seem to leave state legislative seats outside its purview, and the cited section of the constitution clearly deals with state legislators as well as statewide offices. Importantly, the Voter Information Guide (in the screenshot) mentions Assembly and (state) Senate. Even were it to apply only to statewide (and thus executive) posts, everything else I write in this post still would be valid, albeit for a narrower range of cases. ↩︎
A special election in California to fill an interim vacancy (other than in the case of recall) mandates that if one candidate wins a majority of votes, that candidate is elected; otherwise the contest goes to a top-two runoff. ↩︎
Obviously playing off the concept of a constructive vote of no confidence (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/tag/constructive-vote-of-no-confidence/) in some parliamentary democracies, whereby merely losing a vote moved by the opposition is not sufficient to oust an incumbent government. Instead, the parliamentary majority must elect a specific new government. ↩︎
The biggest flaw that comes to mind when thinking of my own proposal here is that it complicates matters for the party of the officer being recalled. That party has to put up a challenger directly against the incumbent, and the split might make the incumbent more likely to survive in office than under the current procedure. However, I do not think that is a great flaw. I am in favor of making it harder to recall, not easier, and in any case, even with separate recall and replacement votes on the same ballot (as is now the case), the incumbent’s party already faces an acute version of this difficulty. Successful recalls are highly likely to change the party holding the office, and that is probably on balance not a bad feature of the process. My proposed procedure has some advantage in encouraging the party of the officeholder to coordinate (whether on the incumbent or a same-party replacement) in addition to encouraging coordination by the opposing forces (as noted above). ↩︎
I would also be on board with a proposal that calls a special election as I describe here but without my “constructive” provision. That is, simply call a special election, under the current procedures used for such election (see footnote 2), without a separate yes/no recall question. ↩︎

California Governor 2026 (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2026/06/02/california-governor-2026/)
Posted on 02/06/2026 (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2026/06/02/california-governor-2026/) by msshugart (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/author/msshugart/)
Election day is finally here. I will not lament the (temporary) end to mailers and TV ads. The governor’s contest in California this year offers a choice of 61 candidates. And yet it somehow does not seem like much of a choice. We have a STUPID (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2022/06/08/californias-stupid-electoral-system-2022-first-round-edition/) electoral system. This is called a primary but is not. It is simple top two, qualifying the two with the highest vote shares regardless of party. By common understanding, a primary election is a party nominating contest, so it should qualify one from each party (and thus more than two). Terminology aside, the strategic incentives (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2024/03/03/california-2024-first-round-and-adam-schiff-for-senate/) and risk of coordination failure (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2024/08/18/a-coordination-failure-followed-by-a-party-switch-cal-sen-4/)are problematic.
Over the course of the campaign there has been a great deal of consternation in Democratic Party circles about the risk that the many candidates on their side could split the vote and allow two Republicans to make it to the runoff. This never seemed remotely plausible to me, even though the rules certainly make it possible. I expected all along that the higher probability was that, despite the fragmentation on their side, it was likelier that two Democrats would make it.
Given that Republicans struggle to get to even 45% of the vote in statewide contests here (and often do much worse), the two Republicans would have to almost perfectly divide their votes, while no Democrat obtained even half the total Republican share. Even with several arguably “serious” candidates, the possibility that none of them would get more than around 22% of the vote seemed unlikely.
And now as we prepare to start seeing actual results, the polling (https://www.270towin.com/2026-governor-polls/california) has come to suggest (https://calmatters.org/newsletter/governor-race-poll-whos-ahead/) that there is the possibly of a close race for second between Democrat Tom Steyer and Republican Steve Hilton. Xavier Becerra, a Democrat, appears to be leading, although some polls have Hilton in first place. Of course, it is that second slot that matters more than who is first. So unless there is a surprise, it probably will come down to a conventional R vs. D runoff (Becerra and Hilton) or two Democrats (Becerra and Steyer).
In the final stages of the campaign, Steyer started unleashing some quite sharp negative attacks on Becerra. It might have made more sense for him to use his ample fortune to attack Hilton, given this is not a purely intraparty contest and he is probably competing realistically for second place.
By the way, I am very open to having comments on this thread on elections happening in other states today, or other California contests aside from the governor race.

Posted on 04/01/2026 (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2026/01/04/ranked-choice-voting-at-the-county-level-in-california-santa-claras-unique-circumstances/) by msshugart (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/author/msshugart/)
This post is a follow-on to the previous one about a low-turnout runoff in Santa Clara County (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2026/01/02/a-very-low-turnout-runoff-santa-clara-county-assessor-2025/), California. Could the county change the election of its officers to ranked-choice voting (via the alternative vote a.k.a. instant runoff)? Yes, it could. However, it is the only county that currently has this authority. Further, it appears it could switch to STV for its Board of Supervisors.
AB 1227 (https://www.leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240AB1227) of 2023 was passed by the state legislature and signed by the governor and explicitly grants to Santa Clara County the option to adopt ranked-choice voting (RCV) for any or all elected county officers. It allows that either the county’s Board of Supervisors or a county initiative may enact RCV.
The legislation further says, “The ordinance [to adopt RCV] shall specify which county officers shall be elected by this method and whether they shall be elected at large or by or from district, as applicable.” The reference to “at large” surely enables the country to elect the Board or other multi-person bodies in the county by single transferable vote (STV), sometimes called (in the US) proportional ranked-choice voting (PRCV). The first section of the enacted state law–the “findings” section–references cities in California that have adopted STV, such as Albany (https://www.albanyca.gov/Departments/City-Clerk/Ranked-Choice-Voting) and Palm Desert (https://www.palmdesert.gov/our-city/election-information), although it simply refers to their systems as “RCV” without the important detail. (Palm Desert now has two districts, one of which is a single seat using RCV/alternative vote, and the other of which elects four by STV/PRCV.)
Interestingly, the law applies only to Santa Clara County. Moreover, its third of three sections reads, in full: “The Legislature finds and declares that a special statute is necessary and that a general statute cannot be made applicable within the meaning of Section 16 of Article IV of the California Constitution because of the unique circumstances relating to the County of Santa Clara’s interest in having the option to use ranked choice voting in its elections.” (The cited section (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2016.&article=IV) states, “A local or special statute is invalid in any case if a general statute can be made applicable.”)
Therefore, we might say that we have here a case “electoral system pork barrel”! Okay it is not a project, which is what “pork barrel” implies, but a measure regarding electoral systems that provides a benefit only to the geographical region represented by its sponsors. The originally introduced bill did not have that third section, although it did already state its applicability was only to the one county. The introducing member was Assembly Member Evan Low, who at the time represented Assembly District 26, encompassing parts of the Silicon Valley, which is to say a large portion of Santa Clara County. Assembly Member Alex Lee later joined as a co-author; his district encompasses other parts of the county, including part of the city of San Jose.
Curiously, the final chaptered amendment to the state code says that an election under RCV in Santa Clara would have to take place at the same time as the statewide “primary” (i.e., the first round under California’s two-round not-a-primary (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/category/california/top-two-system-not-a-primary/) electoral system used for state and federal offices). It is very strange that it would not be held at the November “general” election. This provision changed through the bill’s legislative process, and I will address the apparent reasons for this below. The initial version did not specify the timing of a potential RCV election in the county. The first amended version in the state Assembly added this tortured phrase: “If a proposal would elect an officer by ranked choice voting through a single election with no possibility of a runoff, the bill would authorize the county to hold that election at the first statewide general election following the statewide primary election at which the election otherwise would be held in accordance with existing law.” An amended version in the state Senate said in somewhat more straightforward language that the county could hold an RCV election at either the “primary” or the “general” while adding that third section quoted above.
A further round of amendments in the Senate saw two members of that chamber join as further coauthors, Josh Becker and David Cortese, both of whom represent–you guessed it–parts of Santa Clara County. However, before its final passage the language to require that any such RCV election in the county be held at the “primary” was included.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem does Prop. 5 solve?
In its current form, a state-level recall ballot asks two questions in sequence: first, whether to remove an elected official, and second, who should immediately replace them. Although removal requires a majority vote, replacement doesn’t; whoever gets the most votes takes office, even if it’s by a small plurality in a crowded field. That mismatch can mean that an officeholder ousted by majority vote can be replaced by someone with far less support, and it gives well-organized interest groups a powerful incentive to instigate a recall in order to install a preferred candidate who wouldn’t have majority support under normal conditions. Prop. 5 fixes that mismatch by removing the replacement question and filling a vacancy under existing succession law instead.

Why is this the best solution?
Prop. 5 is the best solution because it fixes the specific, politically exploitable flaw — the plurality replacement provision — while still maintaining the recall as a powerful tool of direct democracy. Under its provisions, if a governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor, already duly elected by a majority of Californians statewide, steps in. If a recall takes place in the first two years of the term and before the filing deadline for the next statewide election, voters would still get a special election for a permanent successor, with a runoff if needed to achieve a majority. If the recall takes place later in the term, the lieutenant governor would serve out the remainder of an ousted governor’s term, the same as if they were to leave office for some other reason. In the event of a recall of other state-level officers, those offices would be filled under existing vacancy replacement provisions.
Why would Californians want to remove someone from office but forfeit to the governor their current right to immediately choose a successor?
Two corrections worth making: In the event of a gubernatorial recall, it wouldn’t be the governor who gains power but the lieutenant governor, a separately elected constitutional officer who is, by virtue of California’s Constitution, explicitly and deliberately next in the line of succession. Intrinsic to any lieutenant governor’s campaign is the assertion that he or she is most qualified to step in if events so demand. Second, voters aren’t forfeiting a choice: If a governor is recalled early in their term, Californians would still elect a permanent successor by majority through a special election. This is a sensible change from the current format, where, in the event of a gubernatorial recall, a replacement candidate can become governor of the largest and most important state in the country with only a small plurality, in a special election decided by a reduced electorate in a low-information and highly politicized environment.
Explain how this empowers majority rule and why that matters.
As it currently stands, while recalling a state-level elected official requires majority support, replacing them doesn’t. Only a plurality is required, which could be as low as 20% in a crowded replacement field. Prop. 5 closes that gap. When a successor election is held, if no one wins a majority outright, it would go to a runoff. So, whoever ultimately holds the office would have secured the support of more than half the voters, not just the largest slice of a fractured field. This is the standard California already applies to nearly every other office and election scenario. A recall shouldn’t be the one process where a candidate can take power without the validation of majority voter support.
How does this measure stop political groups from abusing the recall process?
It removes the existing incentive for political gamesmanship at the expense of electoral integrity. As it stands, a well-funded, motivated minority can force a recall and realistically expect its preferred candidate to win the replacement seat with a small plurality, sometimes far fewer votes than the officeholder who was removed. That’s a low bar for a high-value prize, and it’s why some recalls have been criticized as backdoor attempts to grab a seat that couldn’t be won in a regular election. Prop. 5 raises the bar and removes that incentive: Voters will still be able to remove a corrupt or malfeasant official, but it removes the strategic upside of gaming a plurality-only replacement. Instead, a replacement would be made in the normal order, and in the next election, the winner would ultimately secure a majority, with a runoff if needed.
How would this save taxpayers money?
First and foremost, by changing the incentive structure by eliminating the second question, Prop. 5 would save taxpayers money by reducing the likelihood of hyperpartisan recalls like the one which targeted Gov. Newson in 2021, which cost California taxpayers more than $200 million dollars in the midst of an unprecedented public health emergency where those funds were desperately needed for other purposes. Why is this the best solution?
Prop. 5 is the best solution because it fixes the specific, politically exploitable flaw — the plurality replacement provision — while still maintaining the recall as a powerful tool of direct democracy. Under its provisions, if a governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor, already duly elected by a majority of Californians statewide, steps in. If a recall takes place in the first two years of the term and before the filing deadline for the next statewide election, voters would still get a special election for a permanent successor, with a runoff if needed to achieve a majority. If the recall takes place later in the term, the lieutenant governor would serve out the remainder of an ousted governor’s term, the same as if they were to leave office for some other reason. In the event of a recall of other state-level officers, those offices would be filled under existing vacancy replacement provisions.
Why would Californians want to remove someone from office but forfeit to the governor their current right to immediately choose a successor?
Two corrections worth making: In the event of a gubernatorial recall, it wouldn’t be the governor who gains power but the lieutenant governor, a separately elected constitutional officer who is, by virtue of California’s Constitution, explicitly and deliberately next in the line of succession. Intrinsic to any lieutenant governor’s campaign is the assertion that he or she is most qualified to step in if events so demand. Second, voters aren’t forfeiting a choice: If a governor is recalled early in their term, Californians would still elect a permanent successor by majority through a special election. This is a sensible change from the current format, where, in the event of a gubernatorial recall, a replacement candidate can become governor of the largest and most important state in the country with only a small plurality, in a special election decided by a reduced electorate in a low-information and highly politicized environment.
Explain how this empowers majority rule and why that matters.
As it currently stands, while recalling a state-level elected official requires majority support, replacing them doesn’t. Only a plurality is required, which could be as low as 20% in a crowded replacement field. Prop. 5 closes that gap. When a successor election is held, if no one wins a majority outright, it would go to a runoff. So, whoever ultimately holds the office would have secured the support of more than half the voters, not just the largest slice of a fractured field. This is the standard California already applies to nearly every other office and election scenario. A recall shouldn’t be the one process where a candidate can take power without the validation of majority voter support.
How does this measure stop political groups from abusing the recall process?
It removes the existing incentive for political gamesmanship at the expense of electoral integrity. As it stands, a well-funded, motivated minority can force a recall and realistically expect its preferred candidate to win the replacement seat with a small plurality, sometimes far fewer votes than the officeholder who was removed. That’s a low bar for a high-value prize, and it’s why some recalls have been criticized as backdoor attempts to grab a seat that couldn’t be won in a regular election. Prop. 5 raises the bar and removes that incentive: Voters will still be able to remove a corrupt or malfeasant official, but it removes the strategic upside of gaming a plurality-only replacement. Instead, a replacement would be made in the normal order, and in the next election, the winner would ultimately secure a majority, with a runoff if needed.
How would this save taxpayers money?
First and foremost, by changing the incentive structure by eliminating the second question, Prop. 5 would save taxpayers money by reducing the likelihood of hyperpartisan recalls like the one which targeted Gov. Newson in 2021, which cost California taxpayers more than $200 million dollars in the midst of an unprecedented public health emergency where those funds were desperately needed for other purposes. Measure to reform the California recall process (YES ON PROP 5) (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2026/10/21/measure-to-reform-the-california-recall-process-yes-on-5/)
Posted on 21/10/2026 (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2026/10/21/measure-to-reform-the-california-recall-process-yes-on-5/) by msshugart (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/author/msshugart/)
In this November’s election, Californians are presented with a proposed state constitutional amendment to reform the process of recalling and replacing elected officeholders. It was placed on the ballot by the state legislature as Proposition 5. I am in favor, and I urge California voters to support it. Below are some excerpts from the voter guide (you can access the whole thing via a click here (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/)).
The main defect in the current process that Prop. 5 would fix is the situation whereby a replacement candidate can be elected with less than a majority, and potentially fewer votes than the NO (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2021/08/15/californias-recall-replacement-rules-are-terrible-but-are-they-unconstitutional/) on the recall (i.e., preferring the incumbent remain in office). The state constitution mandates that offices be filled by majority vote, but makes an exception for the replacement for a recalled officer, who must win only a plurality of votes (contingent on YES having a majority for recall). In an earlier post (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2021/09/15/reforming-the-california-recall-replacement-process/) on this problem, I quoted the specific constitutional provisions. A YES on 5 would directly correct this defect.
Under the proposal in Prop. 5, the office becomes vacant and is filled the same way it would be under current provisions if the officer left the post for any other reason (resigning to take another office, death, etc.): special election or appointment, depending on the office. The exception to this generalization of the impact of Prop. 5 is in the right column of the above table: the case of a Governor being recalled. We have a (separately elected) Lieutenant Governor and that officeholder would replace a recalled Governor. However, if the recall takes place in a period leading up to what would be the midterm election of the incumbent’s term (provided it is before candidate-filing deadline), there would be a special election to fill the remainder of the term. This is a sensible provision.
This measure is not perfect, but it is an improvement over the status quo. No longer would a replacement potentially be elected by a plurality instead of a majority. The biggest flaw I see is that in the case of some offices, such as state legislative seats, 1 it would extend the period of vacancy following a recall, and it would necessitate up to two additional elections to fill the seat. 2
There are other ways that the recall–replacement process could be changed to resolve the current problem that this proposition would correct, without creating the new problem I identified of longer vacancies and additional special elections. I went over several of these in the earlier post on reforming the California recall–replacement process (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2021/09/15/reforming-the-california-recall-replacement-process/). (That post was mainly focused on gubernatorial recalls, and I am happy with the Prop. 5 solution on these; the points I made on suggested reforms are generalizable to other contests as well.)
My main suggestion would be to abolish the separate recall election and simply call a special election when the recall petition has been qualified. If the incumbent were to run to defend his or her seat, the incumbent survives in office simply by winning a plurality of the vote. I call this a “constructive recall.” 3 This encourages the opponents to coordinate before the election, and if they fail, their recall bid fails. If a potential replacement candidate wins a majority, he or she is elected and sworn in immediately. If a potential replacement candidate wins only a plurality, then there is a runoff between the candidates with the two highest vote totals. (At least that is how I would do it as long as we use the “top two (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/category/california/top-two-system-not-a-primary/)” system for regular elections. As I have said many times, I dislike that, but that is a separate discussion and one I have addressed in detail (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2024/08/16/unified-primaries-and-rcv-as-steps-towards-us-house-pr-and-what-about-resistance-to-list-pr/#f5219553-9421-4847-ab31-4699862375a9-link) previously.) No proposed process would be without flaws, 4 but I think something like what I propose here would be better. 5 Nonetheless, what is actually before the voters as Proposition 5 in this election is an improvement on the status quo. So I hope YES on PROP 5 wins.
While we are on the topic of measures concerning election rules on this ballot, I also advocate NO on 43 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) , which if passed would raise to two thirds the vote percentage required for a municipal initiative that would propose or increase taxes for a specific purpose. I am against increasing minority-veto provisions such as this.
________
Other resources on Prop. 5: The yes campaign (https://fixtherecall.com/#press) website, LA Time (https://www.latimes.com/politics/newsletter/2026-09-09/california-recall-election-reform-proposition-5)s op-ed, SacBee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316600442.html) op-ed.
________
The ballot title for the proposition says that it “Changes the recall election process for statewide officers.” However, the text does not seem to leave state legislative seats outside its purview, and the cited section of the constitution clearly deals with state legislators as well as statewide offices. Importantly, the Voter Information Guide (in the screenshot) mentions Assembly and (state) Senate. Even were it to apply only to statewide (and thus executive) posts, everything else I write in this post still would be valid, albeit for a narrower range of cases. ↩︎
A special election in California to fill an interim vacancy (other than in the case of recall) mandates that if one candidate wins a majority of votes, that candidate is elected; otherwise the contest goes to a top-two runoff. ↩︎
Obviously playing off the concept of a constructive vote of no confidence (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/tag/constructive-vote-of-no-confidence/) in some parliamentary democracies, whereby merely losing a vote moved by the opposition is not sufficient to oust an incumbent government. Instead, the parliamentary majority must elect a specific new government. ↩︎
The biggest flaw that comes to mind when thinking of my own proposal here is that it complicates matters for the party of the officer being recalled. That party has to put up a challenger directly against the incumbent, and the split might make the incumbent more likely to survive in office than under the current procedure. However, I do not think that is a great flaw. I am in favor of making it harder to recall, not easier, and in any case, even with separate recall and replacement votes on the same ballot (as is now the case), the incumbent’s party already faces an acute version of this difficulty. Successful recalls are highly likely to change the party holding the office, and that is probably on balance not a bad feature of the process. My proposed procedure has some advantage in encouraging the party of the officeholder to coordinate (whether on the incumbent or a same-party replacement) in addition to encouraging coordination by the opposing forces (as noted above). ↩︎
I would also be on board with a proposal that calls a special election as I describe here but without my “constructive” provision. That is, simply call a special election, under the current procedures used for such election (see footnote 2), without a separate yes/no recall question. ↩︎

California Governor 2026 (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2026/06/02/california-governor-2026/)
Posted on 02/06/2026 (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2026/06/02/california-governor-2026/) by msshugart (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/author/msshugart/)
Election day is finally here. I will not lament the (temporary) end to mailers and TV ads. The governor’s contest in California this year offers a choice of 61 candidates. And yet it somehow does not seem like much of a choice. We have a STUPID (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2022/06/08/californias-stupid-electoral-system-2022-first-round-edition/) electoral system. This is called a primary but is not. It is simple top two, qualifying the two with the highest vote shares regardless of party. By common understanding, a primary election is a party nominating contest, so it should qualify one from each party (and thus more than two). Terminology aside, the strategic incentives (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2024/03/03/california-2024-first-round-and-adam-schiff-for-senate/) and risk of coordination failure (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2024/08/18/a-coordination-failure-followed-by-a-party-switch-cal-sen-4/)are problematic.
Over the course of the campaign there has been a great deal of consternation in Democratic Party circles about the risk that the many candidates on their side could split the vote and allow two Republicans to make it to the runoff. This never seemed remotely plausible to me, even though the rules certainly make it possible. I expected all along that the higher probability was that, despite the fragmentation on their side, it was likelier that two Democrats would make it.
Given that Republicans struggle to get to even 45% of the vote in statewide contests here (and often do much worse), the two Republicans would have to almost perfectly divide their votes, while no Democrat obtained even half the total Republican share. Even with several arguably “serious” candidates, the possibility that none of them would get more than around 22% of the vote seemed unlikely.
And now as we prepare to start seeing actual results, the polling (https://www.270towin.com/2026-governor-polls/california) has come to suggest (https://calmatters.org/newsletter/governor-race-poll-whos-ahead/) that there is the possibly of a close race for second between Democrat Tom Steyer and Republican Steve Hilton. Xavier Becerra, a Democrat, appears to be leading, although some polls have Hilton in first place. Of course, it is that second slot that matters more than who is first. So unless there is a surprise, it probably will come down to a conventional R vs. D runoff (Becerra and Hilton) or two Democrats (Becerra and Steyer).
In the final stages of the campaign, Steyer started unleashing some quite sharp negative attacks on Becerra. It might have made more sense for him to use his ample fortune to attack Hilton, given this is not a purely intraparty contest and he is probably competing realistically for second place.
By the way, I am very open to having comments on this thread on elections happening in other states today, or other California contests aside from the governor race.

Ranked choice voting at the county level in California: Santa Clara’s “unique circumstances” (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2026/01/04/ranked-choice-voting-at-the-county-level-in-california-santa-claras-unique-circumstances/)
Posted on 04/01/2026 (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2026/01/04/ranked-choice-voting-at-the-county-level-in-california-santa-claras-unique-circumstances/) by msshugart (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/author/msshugart/)
This post is a follow-on to the previous one about a low-turnout runoff in Santa Clara County (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/2026/01/02/a-very-low-turnout-runoff-santa-clara-county-assessor-2025/), California. Could the county change the election of its officers to ranked-choice voting (via the alternative vote a.k.a. instant runoff)? Yes, it could. However, it is the only county that currently has this authority. Further, it appears it could switch to STV for its Board of Supervisors.
AB 1227 (https://www.leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240AB1227) of 2023 was passed by the state legislature and signed by the governor and explicitly grants to Santa Clara County the option to adopt ranked-choice voting (RCV) for any or all elected county officers. It allows that either the county’s Board of Supervisors or a county initiative may enact RCV.
The legislation further says, “The ordinance [to adopt RCV] shall specify which county officers shall be elected by this method and whether they shall be elected at large or by or from district, as applicable.” The reference to “at large” surely enables the country to elect the Board or other multi-person bodies in the county by single transferable vote (STV), sometimes called (in the US) proportional ranked-choice voting (PRCV). The first section of the enacted state law–the “findings” section–references cities in California that have adopted STV, such as Albany (https://www.albanyca.gov/Departments/City-Clerk/Ranked-Choice-Voting) and Palm Desert (https://www.palmdesert.gov/our-city/election-information), although it simply refers to their systems as “RCV” without the important detail. (Palm Desert now has two districts, one of which is a single seat using RCV/alternative vote, and the other of which elects four by STV/PRCV.)
Interestingly, the law applies only to Santa Clara County. Moreover, its third of three sections reads, in full: “The Legislature finds and declares that a special statute is necessary and that a general statute cannot be made applicable within the meaning of Section 16 of Article IV of the California Constitution because of the unique circumstances relating to the County of Santa Clara’s interest in having the option to use ranked choice voting in its elections.” (The cited section (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2016.&article=IV) states, “A local or special statute is invalid in any case if a general statute can be made applicable.”)
Therefore, we might say that we have here a case “electoral system pork barrel”! Okay it is not a project, which is what “pork barrel” implies, but a measure regarding electoral systems that provides a benefit only to the geographical region represented by its sponsors. The originally introduced bill did not have that third section, although it did already state its applicability was only to the one county. The introducing member was Assembly Member Evan Low, who at the time represented Assembly District 26, encompassing parts of the Silicon Valley, which is to say a large portion of Santa Clara County. Assembly Member Alex Lee later joined as a co-author; his district encompasses other parts of the county, including part of the city of San Jose.
Curiously, the final chaptered amendment to the state code says that an election under RCV in Santa Clara would have to take place at the same time as the statewide “primary” (i.e., the first round under California’s two-round not-a-primary (https://fruitsandvotes.wordpress.com/category/california/top-two-system-not-a-primary/) electoral system used for state and federal offices). It is very strange that it would not be held at the November “general” election. This provision changed through the bill’s legislative process, and I will address the apparent reasons for this below. The initial version did not specify the timing of a potential RCV election in the county. The first amended version in the state Assembly added this tortured phrase: “If a proposal would elect an officer by ranked choice voting through a single election with no possibility of a runoff, the bill would authorize the county to hold that election at the first statewide general election following the statewide primary election at which the election otherwise would be held in accordance with existing law.” An amended version in the state Senate said in somewhat more straightforward language that the county could hold an RCV election at either the “primary” or the “general” while adding that third section quoted above.
A further round of amendments in the Senate saw two members of that chamber join as further coauthors, Josh Becker and David Cortese, both of whom represent–you guessed it–parts of Santa Clara County. However, before its final passage the language to require that any such RCV election in the county be held at the “primary” was included.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 4:33 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:07 PM PST
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem does Prop. 5 solve?
In its current form, a state-level recall ballot asks two questions in sequence: first, whether to remove an elected official, and second, who should immediately replace them. Although removal requires a majority vote, replacement doesn’t; whoever gets the most votes takes office, even if it’s by a small plurality in a crowded field. That mismatch can mean that an officeholder ousted by majority vote can be replaced by someone with far less support, and it gives well-organized interest groups a powerful incentive to instigate a recall in order to install a preferred candidate who wouldn’t have majority support under normal conditions. Prop. 5 fixes that mismatch by removing the replacement question and filling a vacancy under existing succession law instead.
Related Articles
We asked the No on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
Why is this the best solution?
Prop. 5 is the best solution because it fixes the specific, politically exploitable flaw — the plurality replacement provision — while still maintaining the recall as a powerful tool of direct democracy. Under its provisions, if a governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor, already duly elected by a majority of Californians statewide, steps in. If a recall takes place in the first two years of the term and before the filing deadline for the next statewide election, voters would still get a special election for a permanent successor, with a runoff if needed to achieve a majority. If the recall takes place later in the term, the lieutenant governor would serve out the remainder of an ousted governor’s term, the same as if they were to leave office for some other reason. In the event of a recall of other state-level officers, those offices would be filled under existing vacancy replacement provisions.
Why would Californians want to remove someone from office but forfeit to the governor their current right to immediately choose a successor?
Two corrections worth making: In the event of a gubernatorial recall, it wouldn’t be the governor who gains power but the lieutenant governor, a separately elected constitutional officer who is, by virtue of California’s Constitution, explicitly and deliberately next in the line of succession. Intrinsic to any lieutenant governor’s campaign is the assertion that he or she is most qualified to step in if events so demand. Second, voters aren’t forfeiting a choice: If a governor is recalled early in their term, Californians would still elect a permanent successor by majority through a special election. This is a sensible change from the current format, where, in the event of a gubernatorial recall, a replacement candidate can become governor of the largest and most important state in the country with only a small plurality, in a special election decided by a reduced electorate in a low-information and highly politicized environment.
Explain how this empowers majority rule and why that matters.
As it currently stands, while recalling a state-level elected official requires majority support, replacing them doesn’t. Only a plurality is required, which could be as low as 20% in a crowded replacement field. Prop. 5 closes that gap. When a successor election is held, if no one wins a majority outright, it would go to a runoff. So, whoever ultimately holds the office would have secured the support of more than half the voters, not just the largest slice of a fractured field. This is the standard California already applies to nearly every other office and election scenario. A recall shouldn’t be the one process where a candidate can take power without the validation of majority voter support.
How does this measure stop political groups from abusing the recall process?
It removes the existing incentive for political gamesmanship at the expense of electoral integrity. As it stands, a well-funded, motivated minority can force a recall and realistically expect its preferred candidate to win the replacement seat with a small plurality, sometimes far fewer votes than the officeholder who was removed. That’s a low bar for a high-value prize, and it’s why some recalls have been criticized as backdoor attempts to grab a seat that couldn’t be won in a regular election. Prop. 5 raises the bar and removes that incentive: Voters will still be able to remove a corrupt or malfeasant official, but it removes the strategic upside of gaming a plurality-only replacement. Instead, a replacement would be made in the normal order, and in the next election, the winner would ultimately secure a majority, with a runoff if needed.
How would this save taxpayers money?
First and foremost, by changing the incentive structure by eliminating the second question, Prop. 5 would save taxpayers money by reducing the likelihood of hyperpartisan recalls like the one which targeted Gov. Newson in 2021, which cost California taxpayers more than $200 million dollars in the midst of an unprecedented public health emergency where those funds were desperately needed for other purposes. Isn’t ranked choice voting a better solution — since it lets voters immediately elect a majority-backed replacement?
It’s a reasonable idea, but it would require every California county to adopt new voting systems, ballot designs and tabulation processes for a scenario, a statewide recall, that arises only a handful of times a decade. Prop. 5 doesn’t hand anyone new power: For governor, the lieutenant governor, already elected statewide, fills the seat temporarily or for the remainder of the term, and where a special election is required, it’s decided by majority with a runoff. That’s a narrower, immediately workable fix to the specific plurality loophole. RCV is worthy of its own debate, especially in light of recent discussions about abandoning the top-two system, but it isn’t on this ballot, and it isn’t a substitute for closing the gap Prop. 5 targets now.
What is the biggest misconception about this proposition?
That the lieutenant governor automatically becomes governor for the rest of the term in every recall. That’s only true in the back half of a term, or once the filing deadline for the next statewide race has passed. Earlier in a term, voters still elect the permanent successor directly, by majority, in a special election. The other misconception is that this change would somehow take power away from voters generally. It won’t. Voters can still decide whether to recall someone, and, where a recall vote is triggered, the replacement process would insulate this important democratic right from partisan distortion and destructive political gamesmanship.
What are we missing? What didn’t we ask?
The world, and especially politics, have changed a great deal since the adoption of the recall, referendum and the initiative more than 100 years ago. Since that time, politics has gotten meaner, more sophisticated and ever-more gameable by effectively the same moneyed interests that the recall was designed to thwart in the Progressive Era. So, it’s worth asking: What happens if this doesn’t pass? The plurality-replacement loophole stays open indefinitely, effectively guaranteeing a repeat of 2021 at some point. The California Democratic Party, the League of Women Voters of California, California Common Cause, the State Building and Construction Trades Council and the California Labor Federation all support Prop. 5 with the same objective in mind: ensuring that recall outcomes reflect and serve the true will of the voters. It’s worth asking how this differs for legislative recalls versus the governorship specifically, since the succession mechanics for those seats aren’t identical.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 4:32 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:07 PM PST

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
What problem would Prop. 5 create?
A disincentive for the people to self-govern, leading to more distrust of government and restlessness of the “masses.” After a time of withdrawal and lack of participation, the people will feel and react to their oppression in a negative way. Oppressed people eventually revolt, and it’s never pretty.

Currently, the recall process allows a candidate to win office without a majority. Why is that a system not worth reforming?
Under the current system, the democratic process of self-governance is served, and infinite amounts of taxpayer funds are saved by the current one-step process.
Prop. 5 “reforms” the current process by taking power from the people, and — worse — punishing the people for having the audacity to self-govern.
In the case of a recall, the term of office is limited to the remainder of the term of the recalled individual, and awarding the win to the person receiving a plurality in a crowded field is much more protective of the “democratic process” than adopting the changes proposed by Prop. 5, where the Sacramento insiders are the winners, hundreds of millions of dollars are wasted, and democracy dies.
If this measure isn’t a solution for fixing the recall process, do you have an alternate proposal?
This question pre-supposes the recall process needs fixing. The current process, wherein a recall decision and a filling of the recalled position in the case of recall success on the same ballot is efficient, fiscally responsible and respectful to the public.
The suggestion that the cost of having part two of the recall ballot is negligible, let alone millions of dollars, is patently absurd. Also absurd is the Prop. 5 proposal to eventually fill the recalled position with another, delayed election. The cost of a second election, which is likely to lead to a runoff costing more millions, is unarguable. That’s the very definition of absurd.
To quote Sen. Jones, “Our recall process is only ‘broke’ for those who find themselves on the business end of it, like Proposition 5’s author did when he (voted to raise) taxes after breaking campaign promises.”
What’s the biggest misconception about Prop. 5?
That there’s something wrong with the current system, and that CA legislators have any respect for a government of, by and for the people. CA is no longer a republic, but a socialist oligarchy. The power of the people to govern themselves has been so diminished already as to be virtually eliminated, and Prop. 5 is another step to seal the deal for complete power of the elite.
What did we miss? What didn’t we ask that our readers should know?
The element of Prop. 5 dealing with gubernatorial succession is also faulty. Yes, the people ostensibly elected a lieutenant governor, to serve as governor in the event of incapacity or death of the elected governor, not in the event of the governor’s disgrace — by which the lieutenant governor is surely tainted.
If the lieutenant governor wishes to succeed the governor in the event of a recall, that person may appear on the second portion of the ballot.
Chances are virtually 100% that if the people have grown disenchanted with the governor’s performance, they will be equally unwilling to be represented in that office by the second in command — almost certainly complicit in every act of disappointment and betrayal by the governor.

Isn’t ranked choice voting a better solution — since it lets voters immediately elect a majority-backed replacement?
It’s a reasonable idea, but it would require every California county to adopt new voting systems, ballot designs and tabulation processes for a scenario, a statewide recall, that arises only a handful of times a decade. Prop. 5 doesn’t hand anyone new power: For governor, the lieutenant governor, already elected statewide, fills the seat temporarily or for the remainder of the term, and where a special election is required, it’s decided by majority with a runoff. That’s a narrower, immediately workable fix to the specific plurality loophole. RCV is worthy of its own debate, especially in light of recent discussions about abandoning the top-two system, but it isn’t on this ballot, and it isn’t a substitute for closing the gap Prop. 5 targets now.
What is the biggest misconception about this proposition?
That the lieutenant governor automatically becomes governor for the rest of the term in every recall. That’s only true in the back half of a term, or once the filing deadline for the next statewide race has passed. Earlier in a term, voters still elect the permanent successor directly, by majority, in a special election. The other misconception is that this change would somehow take power away from voters generally. It won’t. Voters can still decide whether to recall someone, and, where a recall vote is triggered, the replacement process would insulate this important democratic right from partisan distortion and destructive political gamesmanship.
What are we missing? What didn’t we ask?
The world, and especially politics, have changed a great deal since the adoption of the recall, referendum and the initiative more than 100 years ago. Since that time, politics has gotten meaner, more sophisticated and ever-more gameable by effectively the same moneyed interests that the recall was designed to thwart in the Progressive Era. So, it’s worth asking: What happens if this doesn’t pass? The plurality-replacement loophole stays open indefinitely, effectively guaranteeing a repeat of 2021 at some point. The California Democratic Party, the League of Women Voters of California, California Common Cause, the State Building and Construction Trades Council and the California Labor Federation all support Prop. 5 with the same objective in mind: ensuring that recall outcomes reflect and serve the true will of the voters. It’s worth asking how this differs for legislative recalls versus the governorship specifically, since the succession mechanics for those seats aren’t identical.

Isn’t ranked choice voting a better solution — since it lets voters immediately elect a majority-backed replacement?
It’s a reasonable idea, but it would require every California county to adopt new voting systems, ballot designs and tabulation processes for a scenario, a statewide recall, that arises only a handful of times a decade. Prop. 5 doesn’t hand anyone new power: For governor, the lieutenant governor, already elected statewide, fills the seat temporarily or for the remainder of the term, and where a special election is required, it’s decided by majority with a runoff. That’s a narrower, immediately workable fix to the specific plurality loophole. RCV is worthy of its own debate, especially in light of recent discussions about abandoning the top-two system, but it isn’t on this ballot, and it isn’t a substitute for closing the gap Prop. 5 targets now.
What is the biggest misconception about this proposition?
That the lieutenant governor automatically becomes governor for the rest of the term in every recall. That’s only true in the back half of a term, or once the filing deadline for the next statewide race has passed. Earlier in a term, voters still elect the permanent successor directly, by majority, in a special election. The other misconception is that this change would somehow take power away from voters generally. It won’t. Voters can still decide whether to recall someone, and, where a recall vote is triggered, the replacement process would insulate this important democratic right from partisan distortion and destructive political gamesmanship.
What are we missing? What didn’t we ask?
The world, and especially politics, have changed a great deal since the adoption of the recall, referendum and the initiative more than 100 years ago. Since that time, politics has gotten meaner, more sophisticated and ever-more gameable by effectively the same moneyed interests that the recall was designed to thwart in the Progressive Era. So, it’s worth asking: What happens if this doesn’t pass? The plurality-replacement loophole stays open indefinitely, effectively guaranteeing a repeat of 2021 at some point. The California Democratic Party, the League of Women Voters of California, California Common Cause, the State Building and Construction Trades Council and the California Labor Federation all support Prop. 5 with the same objective in mind: ensuring that recall outcomes reflect and serve the true will of the voters. It’s worth asking how this differs for legislative recalls versus the governorship specifically, since the succession mechanics for those seats aren’t identical.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 4:32 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:07 PM PST
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
What problem would Prop. 5 create?
A disincentive for the people to self-govern, leading to more distrust of government and restlessness of the “masses.” After a time of withdrawal and lack of participation, the people will feel and react to their oppression in a negative way. Oppressed people eventually revolt, and it’s never pretty.

Currently, the recall process allows a candidate to win office without a majority. Why is that a system not worth reforming?
Under the current system, the democratic process of self-governance is served, and infinite amounts of taxpayer funds are saved by the current one-step process.
Prop. 5 “reforms” the current process by taking power from the people, and — worse — punishing the people for having the audacity to self-govern.
In the case of a recall, the term of office is limited to the remainder of the term of the recalled individual, and awarding the win to the person receiving a plurality in a crowded field is much more protective of the “democratic process” than adopting the changes proposed by Prop. 5, where the Sacramento insiders are the winners, hundreds of millions of dollars are wasted, and democracy dies.
If this measure isn’t a solution for fixing the recall process, do you have an alternate proposal?
This question pre-supposes the recall process needs fixing. The current process, wherein a recall decision and a filling of the recalled position in the case of recall success on the same ballot is efficient, fiscally responsible and respectful to the public.
The suggestion that the cost of having part two of the recall ballot is negligible, let alone millions of dollars, is patently absurd. Also absurd is the Prop. 5 proposal to eventually fill the recalled position with another, delayed election. The cost of a second election, which is likely to lead to a runoff costing more millions, is unarguable. That’s the very definition of absurd.
To quote Sen. Jones, “Our recall process is only ‘broke’ for those who find themselves on the business end of it, like Proposition 5’s author did when he (voted to raise) taxes after breaking campaign promises.”
What’s the biggest misconception about Prop. 5?
That there’s something wrong with the current system, and that CA legislators have any respect for a government of, by and for the people. CA is no longer a republic, but a socialist oligarchy. The power of the people to govern themselves has been so diminished already as to be virtually eliminated, and Prop. 5 is another step to seal the deal for complete power of the elite.
What did we miss? What didn’t we ask that our readers should know?
The element of Prop. 5 dealing with gubernatorial succession is also faulty. Yes, the people ostensibly elected a lieutenant governor, to serve as governor in the event of incapacity or death of the elected governor, not in the event of the governor’s disgrace — by which the lieutenant governor is surely tainted.
If the lieutenant governor wishes to succeed the governor in the event of a recall, that person may appear on the second portion of the ballot.
Chances are virtually 100% that if the people have grown disenchanted with the governor’s performance, they will be equally unwilling to be represented in that office by the second in command — almost certainly complicit in every act of disappointment and betrayal by the governor.
