By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 4:32 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:07 PM PST
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
What problem would Prop. 5 create?
A disincentive for the people to self-govern, leading to more distrust of government and restlessness of the “masses.” After a time of withdrawal and lack of participation, the people will feel and react to their oppression in a negative way. Oppressed people eventually revolt, and it’s never pretty.

Currently, the recall process allows a candidate to win office without a majority. Why is that a system not worth reforming?
Under the current system, the democratic process of self-governance is served, and infinite amounts of taxpayer funds are saved by the current one-step process.
Prop. 5 “reforms” the current process by taking power from the people, and — worse — punishing the people for having the audacity to self-govern.
In the case of a recall, the term of office is limited to the remainder of the term of the recalled individual, and awarding the win to the person receiving a plurality in a crowded field is much more protective of the “democratic process” than adopting the changes proposed by Prop. 5, where the Sacramento insiders are the winners, hundreds of millions of dollars are wasted, and democracy dies.
If this measure isn’t a solution for fixing the recall process, do you have an alternate proposal?
This question pre-supposes the recall process needs fixing. The current process, wherein a recall decision and a filling of the recalled position in the case of recall success on the same ballot is efficient, fiscally responsible and respectful to the public.
The suggestion that the cost of having part two of the recall ballot is negligible, let alone millions of dollars, is patently absurd. Also absurd is the Prop. 5 proposal to eventually fill the recalled position with another, delayed election. The cost of a second election, which is likely to lead to a runoff costing more millions, is unarguable. That’s the very definition of absurd.
To quote Sen. Jones, “Our recall process is only ‘broke’ for those who find themselves on the business end of it, like Proposition 5’s author did when he (voted to raise) taxes after breaking campaign promises.”
What’s the biggest misconception about Prop. 5?
That there’s something wrong with the current system, and that CA legislators have any respect for a government of, by and for the people. CA is no longer a republic, but a socialist oligarchy. The power of the people to govern themselves has been so diminished already as to be virtually eliminated, and Prop. 5 is another step to seal the deal for complete power of the elite.
What did we miss? What didn’t we ask that our readers should know?
The element of Prop. 5 dealing with gubernatorial succession is also faulty. Yes, the people ostensibly elected a lieutenant governor, to serve as governor in the event of incapacity or death of the elected governor, not in the event of the governor’s disgrace — by which the lieutenant governor is surely tainted.
If the lieutenant governor wishes to succeed the governor in the event of a recall, that person may appear on the second portion of the ballot.
Chances are virtually 100% that if the people have grown disenchanted with the governor’s performance, they will be equally unwilling to be represented in that office by the second in command — almost certainly complicit in every act of disappointment and betrayal by the governor.

Isn’t ranked choice voting a better solution — since it lets voters immediately elect a majority-backed replacement?
It’s a reasonable idea, but it would require every California county to adopt new voting systems, ballot designs and tabulation processes for a scenario, a statewide recall, that arises only a handful of times a decade. Prop. 5 doesn’t hand anyone new power: For governor, the lieutenant governor, already elected statewide, fills the seat temporarily or for the remainder of the term, and where a special election is required, it’s decided by majority with a runoff. That’s a narrower, immediately workable fix to the specific plurality loophole. RCV is worthy of its own debate, especially in light of recent discussions about abandoning the top-two system, but it isn’t on this ballot, and it isn’t a substitute for closing the gap Prop. 5 targets now.
What is the biggest misconception about this proposition?
That the lieutenant governor automatically becomes governor for the rest of the term in every recall. That’s only true in the back half of a term, or once the filing deadline for the next statewide race has passed. Earlier in a term, voters still elect the permanent successor directly, by majority, in a special election. The other misconception is that this change would somehow take power away from voters generally. It won’t. Voters can still decide whether to recall someone, and, where a recall vote is triggered, the replacement process would insulate this important democratic right from partisan distortion and destructive political gamesmanship.
What are we missing? What didn’t we ask?
The world, and especially politics, have changed a great deal since the adoption of the recall, referendum and the initiative more than 100 years ago. Since that time, politics has gotten meaner, more sophisticated and ever-more gameable by effectively the same moneyed interests that the recall was designed to thwart in the Progressive Era. So, it’s worth asking: What happens if this doesn’t pass? The plurality-replacement loophole stays open indefinitely, effectively guaranteeing a repeat of 2021 at some point. The California Democratic Party, the League of Women Voters of California, California Common Cause, the State Building and Construction Trades Council and the California Labor Federation all support Prop. 5 with the same objective in mind: ensuring that recall outcomes reflect and serve the true will of the voters. It’s worth asking how this differs for legislative recalls versus the governorship specifically, since the succession mechanics for those seats aren’t identical.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 4:32 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:07 PM PST

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
What problem would Prop. 5 create?
A disincentive for the people to self-govern, leading to more distrust of government and restlessness of the “masses.” After a time of withdrawal and lack of participation, the people will feel and react to their oppression in a negative way. Oppressed people eventually revolt, and it’s never pretty.

Currently, the recall process allows a candidate to win office without a majority. Why is that a system not worth reforming?
Under the current system, the democratic process of self-governance is served, and infinite amounts of taxpayer funds are saved by the current one-step process.
Prop. 5 “reforms” the current process by taking power from the people, and — worse — punishing the people for having the audacity to self-govern.
In the case of a recall, the term of office is limited to the remainder of the term of the recalled individual, and awarding the win to the person receiving a plurality in a crowded field is much more protective of the “democratic process” than adopting the changes proposed by Prop. 5, where the Sacramento insiders are the winners, hundreds of millions of dollars are wasted, and democracy dies.
If this measure isn’t a solution for fixing the recall process, do you have an alternate proposal?
This question pre-supposes the recall process needs fixing. The current process, wherein a recall decision and a filling of the recalled position in the case of recall success on the same ballot is efficient, fiscally responsible and respectful to the public.
The suggestion that the cost of having part two of the recall ballot is negligible, let alone millions of dollars, is patently absurd. Also absurd is the Prop. 5 proposal to eventually fill the recalled position with another, delayed election. The cost of a second election, which is likely to lead to a runoff costing more millions, is unarguable. That’s the very definition of absurd.
To quote Sen. Jones, “Our recall process is only ‘broke’ for those who find themselves on the business end of it, like Proposition 5’s author did when he (voted to raise) taxes after breaking campaign promises.”
What’s the biggest misconception about Prop. 5?
That there’s something wrong with the current system, and that CA legislators have any respect for a government of, by and for the people. CA is no longer a republic, but a socialist oligarchy. The power of the people to govern themselves has been so diminished already as to be virtually eliminated, and Prop. 5 is another step to seal the deal for complete power of the elite.
What did we miss? What didn’t we ask that our readers should know?
The element of Prop. 5 dealing with gubernatorial succession is also faulty. Yes, the people ostensibly elected a lieutenant governor, to serve as governor in the event of incapacity or death of the elected governor, not in the event of the governor’s disgrace — by which the lieutenant governor is surely tainted.
If the lieutenant governor wishes to succeed the governor in the event of a recall, that person may appear on the second portion of the ballot.
Chances are virtually 100% that if the people have grown disenchanted with the governor’s performance, they will be equally unwilling to be represented in that office by the second in command — almost certainly complicit in every act of disappointment and betrayal by the governor.

Now I have a very comprehensive picture. Notably, the official "No" campaign responses were weak/hyperbolic ("CA is no longer a republic, but a socialist oligarchy"), which reduces the credibility of the organized opposition. Meanwhile the strongest opposition came from serious editorial boards (SF Chronicle, Mercury News) focused on one specific flaw: the recalled official can run in the special election.

Let me weigh this carefully.

Key facts established:
1. Prop 5 = SCA 1 (Newman), Resolution Chapter 204, Statutes of 2024. Nov 3, 2026 ballot.
2. It removes the replacement question from state recall ballots.
3. Gubernatorial recall: Lt. Gov becomes Governor; if recalled before the close of the nomination period for the next statewide election during the first two years of the term, a special election (top-two, majority winner) consolidated with the statewide primary/general. Otherwise Lt. Gov finishes the term.
4. Other statewide officers recalled: Governor appoints replacement (existing vacancy process).
5. Legislators recalled: special election called by Governor (existing vacancy process).
6. The constitutional ban on the recalled officer being a candidate is removed — they may run in the special election (but may not be appointed).
7. Also changes who performs recall duties: Secretary of State (instead of Lt. Gov) for a gubernatorial recall; Controller if the SoS is recalled.
8. Fiscal impact: negligible/unknown; could save or cost millions; <0.1% of General Fund.
9. Legislative votes: Senate 32-8, Assembly 59-17 (mostly party line).
10. No money raised on either side; no organized opposition campaign committee.
11. Polls: PPIC Sept 35-59 no; PPIC Oct 45-52 no. Likely to fail.
12. Support: LWV of CA, Common Cause CA, Dan Schnur (former GOP FPPC chair), CA Labor Federation, State Building & Construction Trades Council, CA Democratic Party, Indivisible CA, Sec. State Weber, Lt. Gov. Kounalakis. McClatchy CA editorial boards (Sac Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee, SLO Tribune) — Yes. George Skelton (LA Times) — Yes. Matthew Shugart (leading electoral systems scholar) — Yes.
13. Oppose: CA Republican Party, Reform California (DeMaio), Election Integrity Project CA, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn (?), Senate Minority Leader Brian Jones, Asm. Joe Patterson. SF Chronicle, Mercury News/East Bay Times, San Diego Union-Tribune, OC Register — No.

Now the merits.

The core defect Prop 5 addresses is real and significant: California's Constitution requires majority election for virtually every office, but allows a recalled officer's replacement to win on a mere plurality. Twice this produced the perverse result that the successor had fewer votes than those cast to retain the incumbent:
- 2003: "No recall" 55.4% vs. Schwarzenegger 48.6% of the replacement vote (~31% of all ballots cast). More Californians voted to keep Davis than voted for Schwarzenegger.
- 2018 Newman: "No recall" ~42% vs. Ling Ling Chang ~34%.

That is a genuine democratic legitimacy failure: an official ousted by a majority is replaced by someone with less support than the votes to keep them. Also the plurality rule creates a well-documented strategic incentive: a motivated minority can force a $200M recall to install a candidate who couldn't win a normal election — exactly what happened in 2018 with the "weak gazelle" strategy, which flipped a Senate seat and briefly broke the Democratic supermajority.

Prop 5's fix for the gubernatorial case is genuinely good: a top-two, majority-winner special election consolidated with an existing statewide primary/general (so low incremental cost), with the separately-elected Lt. Governor providing continuity in the interim. That is a strictly better legitimacy outcome than a plurality winner from a 46- or 135-candidate circus.

It also quietly fixes a real conflict of interest: today the Lt. Governor performs the Governor's recall duties (i.e., helps run the recall that would make them Governor). Prop 5 moves that to the Secretary of State.

The main substantive defects:
(a) The recalled officer may run in the special election. This is the strongest objection, raised by the SF Chronicle and Mercury News, and the author couldn't justify it. But how damaging is it really? Consider: the recall still removes them from office immediately; they must then face a fresh, majority-rule election against a full field. That's not "no accountability" — it's actually more demanding than the current system in one respect (they must win a majority, not just benefit from a split opposition). And the current constitutional bar on running is arguably its own defect: it prevents voters from reconsidering. However, the Chronicle's point about incumbents' unlimited recall-defense funds carrying over is fair. Still, I'd rate this a moderate flaw, not fatal — and it's the kind of thing the Legislature could clean up by statute or a later amendment.

Hmm, but actually, wait. Constitutional amendments are hard to fix, and this one specifically strips the constitutional bar. Still, a future SCA could restore it.

(b) Lt. Governor finishes the term if the Governor is recalled late in the term (up to ~2 years with no election). But this mirrors the existing vacancy rule for any other reason (death, resignation) — California already has Lt. Gov succession with no special election for gubernatorial vacancies. So Prop 5 doesn't create a new principle there; it just extends an existing one to recalls. And the "same team" concern is partly mitigated because California elects the Lt. Governor on a separate ballot (historically producing cross-party tickets: Deukmejian/McCarthy, Wilson/Davis).

(c) Other statewide officers recalled → Governor appoints. Again, this is exactly the existing vacancy process for death/resignation. No new principle. But it does mean a recall of, say, the AG produces zero voter input until the next scheduled election, and the Governor picks the successor. That's a real democratic loss relative to today.

(d) Legislative seats vacant for months + possible extra election costs. The LAO says millions per standalone special election, but notes savings too. Net negligible relative to the budget. And the delay argument cuts against the recall's usefulness ("don't vote yes or you'll be unrepresented").

(e) Partisan motivation/effect: Democrats advanced it after 2021; in practice it would have blocked Schwarzenegger in 2003 and blocked Chang in 2018. Since Democrats hold nearly all statewide offices and the Governorship, the succession/appointment machinery currently favors Democrats. This is a legitimate fairness concern about process, even if the underlying legitimacy argument is sound.

Now — the deciding question. Which is worse: a system that can install a leader with less support than the votes to retain the incumbent (and invites well-funded minorities to buy a $200M do-over election), or a system that fills recall vacancies the same way California already fills every other vacancy (succession, appointment, or a majority-runoff special election)?

I think the second is the better system on democratic-principle grounds. The whole rest of California's constitutional order requires majority support to take office; the recall replacement is the sole exception, and it's a bad one. Prop 5 aligns recalls with the state's normal, well-understood vacancy rules rather than inventing anything new. The "voters lose their right to choose" objection is weakened by the fact that for the Governor — the office that matters most — voters still get a direct, majority-rule special election whenever the recall happens in the first half of a term, and the Lt. Governor (separately elected statewide, by majority) is the interim in the meantime.

The strongest con argument (recalled officer may run again) is real but modest, and it applies mainly to legislative seats, which are the least consequential; and it can be fixed by a future amendment. Also, the organized "No" campaign's answers were extremely weak and hyperbolic, and no money has been raised on either side — meaning the opposition is essentially editorial-board-level concern rather than a substantive case.

Also worth weighing: this is low-stakes and rare. Recalls qualify roughly once a decade. So the risk of being wrong either way is small; but on the merits, majority rule for taking office is the right principle, and Prop 5 advances it.

Counterweight I should consider seriously: constitutional amendments should be well-drafted, and this one contains a provision its own author can't defend. Voting no signals that the Legislature should come back with a clean version (e.g., keep the replacement question but require a majority/runoff, or raise signature thresholds). The SF Chronicle explicitly made that case. That's a reasonable position — but it also means preserving a known legitimacy defect for another cycle or more, with no guarantee a better fix ever arrives (momentum already ebbed once, per Politico).

On balance, I'll go with YES. The plurality-successor defect is the more serious and more clearly anti-democratic problem; Prop 5 fixes it, aligns recalls with existing vacancy law, adds a majority-runoff mechanism for gubernatorial successors, and removes the Lt. Governor's conflict of interest in running a gubernatorial recall. The flaws it introduces are secondary and fixable.

PROP
5
CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment. Fiscal Impact: Net fiscal effect unknown. In the event of a recall, savings or costs of millions of dollars to administer the election depending on the office recalled. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy. Instead, vacancies typically would be filled through special elections or appointments, depending on the office and timing.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Proposition 5 restores the recall to its original purpose: removing corrupt officials. It closes the loophole that allows replacements to win with a small fraction of the vote, reducing the politics and costs of future recalls. Endorsed by League of Women Voters of California and California Common Cause. Vote YES
CON
Proposition 5 degrades California’s century-old recall process by limiting voters’ right to select a replacement for recalled officials. Instead, when statewide elected officials are recalled, other politicians would choose a replacement. For lower offices, another costly, taxpayer-funded election would come months later, leaving the office vacant and the people unrepresented.
FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
FOR
Josh Newman
Californians for a Prosperous

PROP
5
CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Election of State Officials. The State Constitution establishes legislative, executive, and judicial state offices. Some state officials represent parts of the state, known as districts. Other state officials, like the Governor or Attorney General, represent the entire state. Voters elect people to represent them in state offices for set terms. For example, a state Assembly Member is elected to a two-year term and the Governor is elected to a four-year term. To run for a state office, candidates must submit specific nomination documents before the election. State law sets when this “nomination period” occurs.
Recall of State Officials. The State Constitution allows voters to remove state officials from office before their term ends through a recall. A recall is an election in which voters are asked whether to remove an official from office. To qualify a recall for the ballot, supporters of the recall must collect a certain number of signatures from the official’s district (or statewide for statewide offices). Since 1913, 11 state recall efforts have qualified for the ballot (nine legislators and two Governors) and six have resulted in an official’s removal from office (five legislators and one Governor).
Two Questions in Recall Elections. In a recall election, voters are asked two questions: (1) whether the official should be removed from office and (2) who should replace the official if removed from office. The number of candidates appearing in the second question varies. For example, there were 135 candidates in the 2003 Governor recall election and 46 candidates in the 2021 Governor recall election. If a state official is recalled, the person who receives the most votes in the second question assumes the office.
Vacant State Offices. State officials may leave office before the end of their term for reasons other than a recall. For example, they may die or resign. When this happens, the office becomes vacant. The process to fill a vacant office varies by office. Typically, a vacant seat in the Assembly or Senate is filled through a special election called by the Governor. The Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor when there is a vacancy in the office of the Governor. Vacancies in other executive offices (for example, the Lieutenant Governor or Attorney General) and the Supreme Court and Courts of Appeal are filled by appointments by the Governor.
Frequency of Elections. Statewide elections in California are scheduled every two years. In scheduled election years, a primary election is held in either March or June, depending on the year, and a general election is held in November. In addition to scheduled elections, the state and local governments may call special elections to address specific issues. For example, the Governor may call a special election to fill a vacant Assembly seat.
Elections Administration in California. County elections officials administer most elections in California. As part of this work, they print and mail ballots and other voting materials to registered voters. Some state agencies also have election-related workload. For example, the Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide .
Paying for State Recall Elections. State law requires the California Department of Finance to work with state and local elections officials to estimate the cost of a recall election for a state office. The department is required to send the estimate to the Legislature. The Legislature reviews the estimate and may provide funding for the election. Any remaining costs are paid by the Secretary of State’s and counties’ budgets.
PROPOSAL
As described below, Proposition 5 changes the recall process to make it like the existing process for filling vacant state offices, except for the process to recall the Governor.
Removes Second Question From Recall Elections. Proposition 5 removes the second question—who should replace a recalled official—from a recall election. This means, in future recall elections, voters would only decide whether to remove an elected official from a state office, not who would replace the official.
Specifies Steps for Filling Vacant Offices. If a state official is recalled, Proposition 5 makes the office of the recalled official vacant. Except for the office of the Governor, Proposition 5 uses the existing process for filling vacancies to fill the office. In the case of an office in the state Senate or Assembly, this means that a replacement typically would be elected through a separate special election. The Governor would choose who would fill a vacancy in any other office (other than office of the Governor).
Creates Separate Process for Filling the Office of the Governor. The process for filling the office of the Governor depends on when the recall occurs. If the Governor is recalled before the close of the nomination period for the next statewide election during the first two years of the term, Proposition 5 says that the Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor until voters elect a new Governor at a future statewide election. If the Governor is recalled later in the term, the Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor for the rest of the term.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Fiscal Effects Depend on Frequency of Recalls and the Offices Recalled. Whether there would be costs or savings compared with today depends on the frequency of future recalls and the offices recalled. A recall of a statewide office (for example, Lieutenant Governor) would affect state elections officials and local elections officials in all 58 counties. A recall of a district-based office (for example, a state Senator or Assembly Member) would only affect state elections officials and local elections officials in those districts.
Potential Costs. Proposition 5 could result in higher costs associated with future recall elections if a special election is necessary to fill the vacant office after a recall. For example, a legislative office made vacant after a recall typically would be filled through a special election. If that special election could not be consolidated with a scheduled election, elections officials would need to run a standalone special election. The cost to state and local elections officials to administer such a special election could be millions of dollars per election.
Potential Savings. Proposition 5 could result in lower costs by removing the second question from the ballot. These savings would occur when a Governor is recalled in the latter part of the term and for other offices where vacancies are filled by appointment. There would be savings because ballots and voting materials would no longer include information about replacement candidates. The amount of savings would depend on how many candidates there would have been on the ballot if the second question remained but could be millions of dollars per election.
Net Effect Depends on Circumstances of Future Recall Efforts. The net fiscal effect is unknown because it depends on future recall elections. Proposition 5 could lead to savings or costs potentially in the range of millions of dollars to administer recall elections. How these savings or costs would be shared by state and county governments would depend on future decisions by the Legislature. This net fiscal effect represents less than one-tenth of 1 percent (0.1 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.)

PROP
5
CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 5
California’s recall process should protect our democracy by allowing for the removal of an elected official who is corrupt or abusing their power. It should never be used as a tactic to ‘redo’ an election as a political or partisan scheme. Proposition 5 will restore the recall to its original purpose by making it fair, democratic, and accountable to the will of the majority.
Under current law, a statewide recall ballot asks voters two questions in sequence:
(1) Should the official be recalled? (2) If so, who should replace them?
By being connected, these two questions create a dangerous loophole. An elected official can be removed by a narrow majority. Then, a candidate listed in question #2 can win the office with far less than 50% of the votes cast in the election. This encourages political actors to target officials they couldn’t defeat in a regular election and to install replacements who lack broad public support.
We saw this play out in the 2021 gubernatorial recall. Voters rejected it decisively. The recall lost by nearly the same number of votes that the Governor won the regular election with. But California taxpayers were forced to spend more than $200 million on an election whose outcome simply reconfirmed what voters had already decided. Nearly 70% of California likely voters called the effort a waste of taxpayer money. And had the recall succeeded, the leading replacement candidate would have taken office with support from only about 28% of all recall voters.
Proposition 5 makes a single, commonsense change: it removes the second question from the recall ballot .
Under Prop. 5, in a state-level recall, voters would decide one very simple and important question: whether an officeholder should be removed. If a majority votes yes, that office becomes vacant and is filled under existing vacancy rules. If a Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would become Governor and if the recall occurs early enough, voters would elect a replacement at the next statewide election; other statewide officers would be filled by appointment under existing rules; legislative seats by special election. No shortcuts, no loopholes, and no replacement candidate winning office without majority voter support.
In most states with recalls, vacancies are already filled by succession or a separate election, not a same-day replacement contest.
By eliminating the second question, Proposition 5 removes the incentive and ability to weaponize recalls as a shortcut for partisan advantage. Recalls could not be gamed to overturn the results of regular elections or install candidates who couldn’t win under normal conditions.
The framers of our recall process intended to safeguard voters against corrupt and unaccountable officials, not to provide a weapon for political operators to undo election results they don’t like. Proposition 5 preserves the recall as a tool for accountability while preventing it from being used to sidestep regular elections and majority rule.
Vote YES on Proposition 5 to protect majority rule, defend taxpayers, and restore California’s recall process back to the voters it was designed to serve.
Lorrel Plimier , Co-President
League of Women Voters of California
Darius L. Kemp , MPA, Executive Director
California Common Cause
Dan Schnur , Former Chair
California Fair Political Practices Commission
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 5
Disregard the mental gymnastics the other side is doing here to tie us in knots and try to make sense of the truly nonsensical.
They say Proposition 5 “protects democracy.” It does the opposite-it erodes one of the fundamental elements of our recall process: to choose who replaces the recalled politician.
That’s not protecting democracy-that’s protecting political elites.
They call California’s system a “dangerous loophole.” It’s worked for 100 years, ousting politicians who abuse their office and replacing them with whoever the voters decide will do better.
Proposition 5 would create a loophole, not close one. The other side is gaslighting you. They think you won’t notice. Don’t be fooled.
If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it. Our recall process is only ‘broke’ for those who find themselves on the business end of it, like Proposition 5’s author did when he raised taxes after breaking campaign promises.
Now, he wants to burn it down on his way out the door-making future recalls less effective and keeping politicians like him less accountable.
If you traded in your car, would you want to know what you were getting in return-or would you be happy to sign it away and let the salesman stick you in a jalopy of their choosing after you’ve already committed? That’s what Proposition 5 asks you to do.
Our recall system will continue to work just fine, if we don’t let political elites with sour grapes tinker with it to their benefit.
Vote NO!
Brian W. Jones , Senate Minority Leader
Joe Patterson , Assemblymember
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 5
Proposition 5 will take away your voice and erode your ability to remove and replace failed or corrupt politicians from office.
California politicians already have too much power. Proposition 5 gives them even more-and it does it by taking power away from you, the voters.
For over 100 years, California’s recall process has given us the ability to remove elected officials who abuse their office, break promises or fail to do the job they were elected to do. And, when that happens, the current process allows you-not politicians-to choose who replaces them.
Proposition 5 changes that system forever and takes power away from the people.
Today, a recall election asks two simple questions: Should the elected official be removed from office? If so, who should replace them? That means Californians can remove a failed politician and immediately choose someone new to take their place.
Proposition 5 keeps the first part but eliminates your ability to vote for a replacement.
Instead, Sacramento political insiders would decide what happens next. In many cases, politicians themselves-not voters-would choose who fills the vacancy, essentially allowing them to appoint another one of their friends or political allies to replace the one you just ousted.
In other cases, rather than an immediate replacement, the seat would sit vacant until another costly election-funded by you, the taxpayer-was scheduled months later. And here’s the kicker; that failed politician you just ran out the door for failure or corruption, they'd be allowed to run in that next election to regain control of the seat they just lost.
In either case, your vote matters less, and the political establishment gains more control.
Californians deserve the right to remove an elected official-and to choose who comes next. Proposition 5 takes away half of that right, and that’s wrong.
Supporters claim this measure improves democracy. It doesn’t. Democracy means voters-not Sacramento politicians-get to choose their leaders, when to give them the boot and who to replace them with. Proposition 5 undermines that fundamental concept.
Ask yourself: if you vote to remove a governor or another statewide elected official, shouldn’t you also decide who replaces them?
The answer is clear.
It’s also worth wondering why this measure is on the ballot in the first place. Why fix a system that isn’t broken and has been working just fine for over a century?
Well, the author of this proposal himself was recalled by California voters when he voted to raise gas taxes after promising not to. Instead of respecting the will of the people, he now wants to rewrite the rules and protect politicians like him from any meaningful accountability. California’s recall belongs to the people-not politicians. Protect your voice. Protect your vote. Protect your right to hold elected officials accountable.
Vote NO on Proposition 5.
Brian W. Jones , Senate Minority Leader
Joe Patterson , Assemblymember
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 5
Don’t be misled. Proposition 5 preserves your power to recall an official by majority vote while closing the loophole that allows a replacement candidate to take office with a small fraction of the vote.
Under current law, voters decide whether to remove an official by majority vote, but the replacement can win with far less than a majority. In 2021, a replacement candidate could have become Governor with support from 28% of recall voters. That is not majority rule.
Opponents want you to believe Proposition 5 takes away your right to choose. It does not. The real question is whether someone should become Governor with support from only a small fraction of California voters.
Proposition 5 preserves the recall while separating the decision to remove an officeholder from the decision about who should serve next. If a Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor-elected statewide by California voters-provides continuity of government until voters choose the next Governor through a regular election. Voters will still choose their elected officials. But candidates seeking statewide office should earn that office in a regular election based on their qualifications, record, and plans for California, not use a recall as a shortcut to power.
A recall should decide whether an officeholder remains in office. Choosing who governs should happen in a regular election, where candidates earn the support of California voters. Proposition 5 protects the recall, respects majority rule, and ensures candidates run on their own merits. Vote YES on Proposition 5.
Lorrel Plimier , Co-President
League of Women Voters of California
Darius L. Kemp , MPA, Executive Director
California Common Cause

**SCA 1 (Resolution Chapter 204, Statutes of 2024) Newman.
Elections: recall of state officers.**
The California Constitution provides that voters may recall a state officer by majority vote and, in the same election, elect a successor with a plurality of the vote.
The Constitution prohibits an officer who is the subject of a recall election from being a candidate for successor.
The Constitution provides that the Lieutenant Governor becomes Governor when a vacancy occurs in the office of Governor, and requires the Lieutenant Governor to act as Governor during the impeachment, absence from the state, or other temporary disability of the Governor or of a Governor-elect who fails to take office.
When a recall of the Governor is initiated, the Constitution requires the Lieutenant Governor to perform the recall duties of the Governor.
The Constitution requires the Governor to fill vacancies in certain judicial and executive offices by appointment, as specified.
This measure would eliminate the successor election for a recalled state officer and instead provide, in the event an officer is removed in a recall election, that the office will remain vacant until it is filled in accordance with the Constitution and statute.

One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials.

Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
Proposition 5: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Recall Reform, Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment
Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023. As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters. The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024. The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process. Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled. If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law. Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor. If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The financial impact would depend on how often recalls occur and which offices are involved. Costs could increase by millions of dollars when a recall creates a vacancy that requires a separate special election, particularly for legislative offices. At the same time, eliminating replacement candidates from recall ballots could save millions in some elections by reducing ballot and election-material costs. Overall, Proposition 5 could result in either costs or savings of potentially millions of dollars per recall election, although the effect would be very small compared with the state’s overall budget.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports changing California’s recall process so voters would decide only whether to remove an official, with the vacancy filled later under state law. A recalled official could run again, and the Lieutenant Governor would generally replace a recalled Governor.
NO: A “no” vote supports keeping the current recall process, in which voters decide whether to remove an official and simultaneously vote on who should replace that official if the recall succeeds.

So the recalled officer CAN run in a special election (but cannot be appointed).

Article II, Section 17: If recall of the Governor OR Secretary of State is initiated, the recall duties of that office shall be performed by the Secretary of State (for Governor) or Controller (for SoS). If both, the Controller. Wait — current law says "If recall of the Governor is initiated, the recall duties of that office shall be performed by the Lieutenant Governor." Under current law, the SoS conducts the election. But if the SoS is recalled, there's a conflict. New: Governor's recall duties → Secretary of State; SoS's recall duties → Controller; both → Controller. Hmm, actually wait. Under current law, when the Governor is recalled, the Lt. Governor performs the Governor's recall duties (e.g., setting the election date). Prop 5 changes it so the Secretary of State does that. That's actually an improvement in some sense — reduces the Lt. Gov's conflict of interest (Lt. Gov would benefit from the Governor's recall). Good detail.

Article V, Section 10(b): If Governor removed by recall, Lt. Governor becomes Governor for remainder of unexpired term. BUT if removed before the close of the nomination period for the next statewide election during the first two years of the Governor's term, a special election shall be called to replace the Governor, consolidated with the statewide primary (top-two if no majority), and winner becomes Governor for remainder of term.

So there IS a special election for the Governor if recalled early in the term (first two years). If recalled in the latter two years, the Lt. Governor serves the rest of the term (up to ~2 years) with no voter input.

Endorsement: Prop 5 has a flaw so bizarre even its author doesn’t like it
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 8, 2026
So much has happened in American politics since 2021 that the recall election of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, which he overwhelmingly defeated, feels like a distant memory.
Proposition 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot puts recalls back in the spotlight.
Endorsement guide: S.F. Chronicle Endorsements for the 2026 California Election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements/)
Also: Y (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)es or no? Here are the Chronicle’s endorsements for California Supreme Court and appeals courts (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)
Authored by (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) former Democratic state Sen. Josh Newman of Fullerton — who was recalled in 2018, won reelection in 2020 and lost again in 2024 — Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

Its judgments are made independent of the news operation , which covers the news without consideration of our editorial positions.
But it is there. And the inability or unwillingness of lawmakers to put forth a simple, clean reform effort is reason enough for voters to reject this measure.
California’s recall process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.

Proposition 5
Delay replacing recalled state officials
Under current law, after choosing whether to recall an elected official, voters are asked who should replace them. This constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by state lawmakers, would delay the election of a successor until a separate election. The recalled officer would be allowed to run in that election. If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over their duties until a new governor is elected. The California Legislature put this measure on the ballot.
Weigh the arguments.
Take our quizzes to learn more about each proposition.
BEGIN → (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/propositions/quizzes)
Support
Oppose
Summary
Support
Proposition 5 is a constitutional amendment born out of a proposal from the secretary of state’s office following the unsuccessful recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. Secretary of State Shirley Weber told lawmakers her office felt a recall election should focus on whether the elected official should be recalled, not whether other potential candidates would be better in the role. Democrat Josh Newman, who was successfully recalled from his state Senate seat in 2018, authored the measure, saying it would reduce the “political gamesmanship” that elevates candidates who otherwise wouldn’t receive a majority of votes.
Oppose
Opponents including the California Republican Party and Election Integrity Project, which advocates for voter ID requirements and restrictions on mail-in voting, argue that allowing the lieutenant governor to assume the governor’s position if the governor were recalled would dissuade people from participating in a recall election. Almost all legislative Republicans also opposed it, arguing that it would dilute the power of voters while protecting incumbents. The current recall process is how former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, was first elected in 2003.

Voters get their say with Prop. 5 by Kate Wolffe (https://calmatters.org/author/kate-wolffe/) October 5, 2026 October 2, 2026 Republish Share this: Share on X (Opens in new window) X (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-election-proposition-5-explainer/) Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-election-proposition-5-explainer/) Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-election-proposition-5-explainer/) Then-gubernatorial candidate Arnold Schwarzenegger celebrates his victory in the California recall election with his wife Maria Shriver at the Century Plaza Hotel in Los Angeles, on Oct. 7, 2003. Photo by NewsBase via AP Photo In summary Following the failed 2021 recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom, Democrats had the political will and momentum to call for changes to the recall process. What emerged was Proposition 5 on the November ballot, a measure to change the recall process. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Sacramento State political science professor Kim Nalder was working out at a Sacramento gym in 2003 when she overheard a conversation about the upcoming recall election of then-Gov. Gray Davis, a Democrat. She remembers “guys in the weight room just saying, like, “How cool would that be to have Arnold Schwarzenegger as our governor?’” she said. “It had nothing to do with policy at all.” A few months later, the international action film star triumphed in a field of 135 candidates to replace Davis, who’d been re-elected the year before but had come under fire for rolling blackouts in the state and unpopular vehicle license fees. “The Governator” went on to serve nearly two terms. If the election were just about whether or not Davis should keep his job, and not also who should replace him if he were recalled, Nalder doubts the Republican Schwarzenegger would ever have taken office. Accompanying him on the ballot were a host of other colorful characters, including actor Gary Coleman and porn star Mary Carey. Per the rules of the recall, the candidate with the most votes, not necessarily the majority, wins. “I just think the recall probably wouldn’t have happened — because there wasn’t that much upset at Davis himself — if we didn’t, you know, have any fun alternatives,” she said. California voters this year are deciding whether to approve Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), which would do away with “the second question” of who should replace a state elected official if they are recalled. Instead, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election. ELECTION 2026 (https://calmatters.org/tag/election-2026) 2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) Get ready for California’s midterm election. This voter guide has everything you need to know The measure was placed on the November ballot by Democratic lawmakers in 2024 with the support of the secretary of state and good governance groups Common Cause and League of Women Voters. It came in response to the 2021 attempted recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing that it would dilute the power of the voters and add costs associated with follow-up special elections. However, with 14 propositions on the ballot and not a dollar raised so far in support or opposition, both sides may have to rely on voters’ gut reactions. The ‘weak gazelle ’ Aside from the recall of Davis, the only other successful state recall this century was that of the author of Prop. 5, Democrat Josh Newman. In 2017, Newman was a freshman lawmaker representing a purple Southern California district when he joined 26 of his colleagues in approving the gas tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article143237054.html), which added a 12 cent surcharge to every gallon of gas purchased in California to fund transportation projects. Republicans fiercely opposed the effort, arguing new taxes weren’t necessary. The bill passed with the bare minimum of votes. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election. Now I have a good picture. Let me also look at the Sacramento Bee editorial in support and the Mercury News / San Diego Union-Tribune / OC Register editorials against, to weigh the arguments. Also check the League of Women Voters' Easy Voter Guide recommendation.

Also, key considerations:

Arguments FOR Prop 5:
1. The two-question recall allows a replacement to win with a plurality — sometimes a small fraction of votes (2021: leading replacement candidate had ~28% of recall voters; 2003: Schwarzenegger won with 48.6% of the replacement vote, but that was ~31% of all ballots cast). This is undemocratic — the replacement could win with far fewer votes than those cast against the recall. In 2003, more people voted "no recall" (55.4%) than voted for Schwarzenegger (48.6% of replacement vote = ~31% of all ballots). That is a genuine democratic legitimacy problem.
2. Simplifies ballot, reduces cost of printing 100+ candidates.
3. Most other states with recalls use succession/special election, not a same-day replacement.
4. Reduces incentive to use recalls as a "redo" of a prior election — i.e., a partisan weapon.
5. Reduces confusion for voters.
6. Also: Prop 5 removes the Lieutenant Governor's conflict of interest in gubernatorial recalls (SoS now performs recall duties instead of the Lt. Gov, who would directly benefit from the Governor's removal). That's a real good-governance improvement.
7. Endorsed by League of Women Voters of California, California Common Cause, Dan Schnur (former FPPC chair, a Republican/independent). Sacramento Bee endorsed.
8. Passed the Legislature with strong bipartisan-ish margins (Senate 32-8, Assembly 59-17).

Arguments AGAINST Prop 5:
1. Takes away voters' right to choose a replacement directly; transfers power to politicians (the Governor appoints replacements for other statewide offices; the Lt. Governor — same ticket effectively — becomes Governor).
2. A recalled officer could run in the special election to regain the seat — a genuinely bizarre provision that weakens the recall's teeth. Even the author couldn't explain it. SF Chronicle rejected the measure primarily on this basis.
3. The Lt. Governor succeeding a recalled Governor could mean the recall produces no policy change — the person most closely aligned with the recalled governor takes over. Though in California the Lt. Gov is elected separately and could be of a different party.
4. If a Governor is recalled late in the term (after the first two years), the Lt. Governor serves out the remainder of the term with no voter input — potentially up to ~2 years.
5. Creates gaps in representation for legislative seats (months vacant) and could cost millions for separate special elections.
6. Partisan motivation: Democrats advanced it after the 2021 Newsom recall scare; it would have prevented Schwarzenegger (R) from becoming Governor in 2003.
7. It doesn't address the actual root problem (low signature threshold, plurality replacement winner) — a better reform would be a runoff requirement for the replacement or raising signature thresholds.
8. Mercury News, San Diego Union-Tribune, OC Register, SF Chronicle opposed.
9. Polling: 45% yes / 52% no (PPIC October) — trending up but below majority.

Let me think about which side is stronger on the merits.

Core question: Is removing the replacement question a net democratic improvement?

The strongest pro argument is real: In 2003, Gray Davis was recalled with 55.4% voting "yes recall" — but Schwarzenegger got only 48.6% of the replacement vote, which was about 31% of all votes cast. That means ~70% of voters did NOT vote for him. And critically, the recall question and the replacement question were decided by different majorities. A candidate who could never win a normal election can win a recall. Also, in 2021, Larry Elder got 45% of replacement votes, which was ~28% of total recall voters.

But is the current system actually worse than the Prop 5 alternative? Under Prop 5:
- Governor recalled late in term → Lt. Governor serves up to 2 years without any election. The Lt. Governor in California is elected separately, so in principle voters chose them statewide. But they are almost always a co-partisan of the governor, and typically from the same administration's wing. So a successful recall could result in zero change of direction — which arguably defeats the purpose.
- Other statewide officers recalled → Governor appoints replacement. So a partisan ally of the incumbent Governor picks the replacement for a recalled officer. Notably, if the recalled officer is, e.g., the Secretary of State or Attorney General (whom voters may have recalled because of misconduct), the Governor appoints the successor. That's a real democratic deficit. Though this mirrors the existing vacancy process.
- Legislators recalled → special election, but the recalled legislator can run again. This is the biggest flaw. A recall that costs millions and results in the same person potentially returning to office is a seriously weakened accountability tool. And under current law, that's expressly prohibited.

So Prop 5 removes a real flaw (plurality replacement winner) but introduces/retains another real flaw (recalled official can run again; Lt. Gov succession with no voter input late in term).

Now, how often does this matter? Recalls are rare — 11 qualified since 1913, 6 succeeded. So the practical stakes are low. The fiscal impact is negligible (<0.1% of General Fund).

Hmm. Let me think about which is the better vote.

Consider the "worst case" scenarios under each:
- Under current law worst case: An official is recalled by 50%+1 and replaced by someone with 28% of recall voters' support — i.e., someone a supermajority of voters didn't want. This actually happened in spirit in 2003 (Schwarzenegger got 31% of all votes cast). Also produces 135-candidate ballot chaos, ~$200M cost.
- Under Prop 5 worst case: A recalled Governor is replaced by the Lt. Governor (a political ally) for up to 2 years without any election; or a recalled legislator wins the special election right back, nullifying the recall; or a recalled statewide officer is replaced by a gubernatorial appointee with no voter input at all.

Actually the "recalled officer can run again" provision is quite damning — it means the recall becomes an expensive opinion poll rather than an actual removal, in the case of legislators. The author himself admitted "I'm honestly not sure... It wouldn't pain me if it wasn't there." That's a drafting failure at the constitutional level, and constitutional amendments are hard to fix.

This is undemocratic — the replacement could win with far fewer votes than those cast against the recall. In 2003, more people voted "no recall" (55.4%) than voted for Schwarzenegger (48.6% of replacement vote = ~31% of all ballots). That is a genuine democratic legitimacy problem.
2. Simplifies ballot, reduces cost of printing 100+ candidates.
3. Most other states with recalls use succession/special election, not a same-day replacement.
4. Reduces incentive to use recalls as a "redo" of a prior election — i.e., a partisan weapon.
5. Reduces confusion for voters.
6. Also: Prop 5 removes the Lieutenant Governor's conflict of interest in gubernatorial recalls (SoS now performs recall duties instead of the Lt. Gov, who would directly benefit from the Governor's removal). That's a real good-governance improvement.
7. Endorsed by League of Women Voters of California, California Common Cause, Dan Schnur (former FPPC chair, a Republican/independent). Sacramento Bee endorsed.
8. Passed the Legislature with strong bipartisan-ish margins (Senate 32-8, Assembly 59-17).

1. Takes away voters' right to choose a replacement directly; transfers power to politicians (the Governor appoints replacements for other statewide offices; the Lt. Governor — same ticket effectively — becomes Governor).

We urge voters to reject it.
Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate on the same ballot as a recall. Currently a recall ballot has two questions: 1) Should the elected official be removed, and 2) Choose a candidate to replace that official if the recall is successful.
The measure would remove question 2, eliminating the simultaneous election for a replacement. Instead, if a state official other than a governor was recalled, the office would become vacant and would be filled by special election or appointment, according to existing law. If a governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over and serve until the end of the term or until a special election could be held, depending on timing.
Under current law, a recalled official is barred from running as a replacement candidate in the special election to fill the seat. Proposition 5 changes that as well. In a special election to replace a recalled official, the recalled official could be on the ballot.
These changes turn a process to remove officials from power into a cynical blueprint to keep power in the hands of the same officials. It makes a mockery of the recall, which was designed to empower voters to remove and immediately replace an officeholder for any reason, whether the officeholder thinks the reason is sufficient or not.
Rejecting Proposition 5 is also about preserving the state’s ability to empower unique and independent political voices.
Under current rules, officials who are recalled are succeeded by the candidate seeking that official’s job who gets the most votes at the same time as the recall. This process is why Arnold Schwarzenegger was able to quickly replace the deeply unpopular Davis.
Nearly one million more Californians voted to recall Davis than to retain him, and the Republican Schwarzenegger won a plurality of the replacement vote after running as a pro-business social liberal who wanted the state to lead the global response (https://www.kqed.org/science/1931206/californias-a-team-on-climate-moonbeam-and-the-governator) to climate change.
But if Proposition 5 had been in place, Davis would have been succeeded by Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante. He was an uninspiring but mostly baggage-free politician who would have likely been the favorite in a subsequent regular or special election in California to finish Davis’ term, even against Schwarzenegger.
Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded candidates — while stripping the people of their primary tool of accountability — is a bad idea.
Reject Proposition 5.

Proposition 5 could change California’s recall elections. Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 8:16 AM
Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html) seeks to fundamentally change how California conducts recall elections for members of the Legislature and constitutional officers elected statewide. Such elections have been rare in California.
According to theLegislative Analyst’s Office, (https://lao.ca.gov/) only 11 state recall efforts targeting nine legislators and two governors have qualified for the ballot since 1913. In 2003, Gray Davis (https://www.modbee.com/opinion/opn-columns-blogs/article251385288.html) became the only California governor to be recalled, a fate that also befell five state legislators over the years. The last statewide recall effort to qualify for the ballot was the unsuccessful campaign to oust Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/editorials/article253266413.html)
Under current law, voters are asked two questions in the same election when a recall effort qualifies for the ballot. The first is whether a state officer should be recalled. The second is who should replace that officer from a field of hopefuls seeking consideration if a recall is successful. In 2003, 135 candidates wanted to succeed Davis. In 2021, there were 46 candidates vying for Newsom’s job.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html)
If Prop. 5 is approved by state voters in November, the second question will be eliminated.
In future statewide recalls that gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot, Californians would only vote yes or no on whether an officer should be recalled. If a state recall of a member of the Legislature was successful, that office would remain vacant until a special election was held. If a constitutional officer were recalled, the vacancies would be filled by the governor. Should a future governor be recalled in the first two years of office, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until a special election was held. If a governor were recalled later in the term, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until the next scheduled election.
This would be a longer process, but also one that’s more thoughtful, deliberate and — most importantly — respects the democratic norm of majority rule.
It’s why our combined editorial boards representing The Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee and San Luis Obispo Tribune endorse Prop. 5.
Recall elections in California
Since California voters approved the recall process in 1911, five replacement candidates have been elected after six officials were removed from office with less than 50% of the vote. In California recall elections, the candidate who receives the most votes wins, unlike in a special election, where a candidate must win a majority.
This creates a conundrum of a recalled official garnering more voter support than the replacement candidate who “wins” the recall.
In the 2018 recall of former stateSen. Josh Newman, for instance, (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article145349124.html) his replacement, Republican Ling Ling Chang, came out on top with just under 34% of the vote. Newman points out that he had more votes in his favor; nearly 42% of voters opposed his recall.
“So I got more votes by way of ‘no, don’t kick him out,’ than she got by ‘yes, please put her in,’” Newman said.
Newman won back his Senate seat in the next regular election and then went on to write Prop. 5 (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-voters-prop-5-changes-recall-election-process/73175034).
One of the proposition’s most outspoken opponents is Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a former talk radio host who pushed for Newman’s recall in 2017.
How Prop. 5 opponents feel
DeMaio sees Prop. 5 as an attempt by the ruling party to evade recalls. “What they want to do is create a situation where politicians trying to fend off a recall can say, ‘Don’t vote for the recall or else you won’t be represented for 12 months. You’ll lose your voice,’” he told us.
Actually, Article II, Section 15 of the California Constitution, says a recall election must be held within 60 and 80 days of recall petition signatures being certified. The election may be held within 180 days of certification if it is consolidated with the next regularly scheduled election.
Arguments against Prop. 5 ignore that the current system created instances where replacement candidates got elected with less than 50% of the vote.
They decry the cost of conducting special elections and oppose that Prop. 5 would allow a recalled official to run in a special election to fill the vacancy.
There have been 182 attempts (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present) to recall state officials in California. Eleven of those made the ballot, and only six were successful.
Some view the current recall system as “a weapon for political operators (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5.pdf) to undo election results they don’t like,” to quote the League of Women Voters and others.
Prop. 5 cannot put an end to the political gamesmanship, but it can safeguard the will of the voters by following the principle of majority rule.
McClatchy Media’s California editorial board strongly urges a “yes” vote on Proposition 5.
